But this parallelism is unstable under interpretive pressure. For beliefs (mind-to-world direction of fit), interpretation threatens authority because believing P requires getting the world right, and the confabulation literature shows we're no better at getting our own minds right than we are at getting the external world right. But for intentions (world-to-mind direction of fit), interpretation enhances rather than threatens authority, because forming an intention partly consists in committing yourself to a course of action, and avowing an intention is itself a way of undertaking that commitment. When I say 'I intend to φ,' I'm not primarily reporting a pre-existing state but binding myself. The interpretive act itself can constitute the intention in a way it cannot constitute belief. This explains why Moran's agentialism works better for intentions than beliefs—and why we should stop treating them as parallel cases.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "defenders of first-person authority" who "treat beliefs and intentions as parallel cases" where both attitudes supposedly have the same kind of special access. But the major theorists in this debate do NOT treat them as straightforwardly parallel. Moran himself distinguishes these attitudes extensively in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001), arguing that self-knowledge of intention works through deliberation about what to do (the "transparency condition") while belief works through deliberation about what's true. Edgley (1969) distinguished practical from theoretical self-knowledge. Even Shoemaker, often cited for first-person authority, explicitly treats conative and cognitive states differently. The thesis presents its insight about direction-of-fit asymmetries as if correcting a widespread error, but this asymmetry is actually common ground. The real debate concerns whether EITHER attitude type enjoys genuine authority and what explains it—not whether they work the same way. The thesis attacks a crude parallelism that serious defenders abandoned decades ago, making this a battle against a position nobody actually holds in the form described.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis may contain valuable insights about direction of fit, but it mischaracterizes the dialectical situation. The observation that intentions and beliefs differ isn't news to the literature it addresses.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *recognizing some differences* with *recognizing the right differences in the right way*. Yes, Moran distinguishes beliefs and intentions—but he still thinks BOTH enjoy first-person authority through their respective transparency conditions. That's the parallelism the thesis targets: the structural assumption that each attitude type has its own route to authority, making them parallel successes rather than asymmetric outcomes.

The thesis claims something stronger and more specific than "they differ." It claims that only intentions survive interpretive pressure because only they have the constitutive feature that makes authority possible under interpretation: the self-fulfilling character of avowal. When I avow an intention, the avowal can *make it so* in a way that avowing a belief cannot. This isn't just "deliberation about what to do vs. what's true"—it's about whether the speech act itself has world-to-mind fit.

Moran's transparency condition for belief still faces the confabulation problem: when I ask "Is P true?" I might get the answer wrong, and then my self-attribution is false. But when I ask "Shall I φ?" and answer "Yes," my avowal "I intend to φ" can constitute the intention even if my prior psychological state was murky. The avowal has performative force for intentions that it lacks for beliefs.

The thesis isn't correcting crude parallelism—it's arguing that even sophisticated accounts like Moran's preserve a deeper parallelism (both attitudes get authority, just through different mechanisms) when they should recognize a fundamental asymmetry (only intentions get authority because only they have the right metaphysics for it). The target is the *structural parallelism of success*, not the *identity of mechanism*.


VERDICT

The defence fails, though not completely.

The defence succeeds in identifying a real distinction: there IS a difference between "these work differently" and "only one actually works." If the literature uniformly granted authority to both attitudes while merely explaining them differently, the thesis would have a genuine target.

But the defence's own citations undermine it. Moran doesn't just say beliefs and intentions work differently—he explicitly worries whether belief gets authority at all, precisely because of the confabulation problem the thesis invokes. His agentialism is widely read as *rescuing* first-person authority for belief by making it more like intention (through rational self-constitution), not as establishing a parallel success.

More fatally: the thesis presents its direction-of-fit point as if it's doing novel work to destabilize the debate, but this is exactly what Edgley's practical/theoretical distinction already captured. The performative character of intention-avowal isn't a hidden resource—it's been explicit since at least Anscombe.

The thesis may be right that intentions survive interpretive pressure better than beliefs. But it cannot claim to be *destabilizing an assumption* when the literature has been explicitly asymmetric for fifty years. At best, it's *taking a side* in an existing asymmetry debate, not exposing a false parallelism.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (TRIVIAL)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to destabilize "the assumption shared by both sides that first-person authority stands or falls together across different attitude types." But this purported assumption is not actually contested ground—it's a verbal repackaging of observations already explicit in the literature. The "direction of fit" distinction comes from Anscombe (1957) and has been standard equipment for 65 years. The claim that intention-avowals have performative or self-fulfilling character appears in Anscombe, is central to Moran's account, and is developed extensively by Bilgrami and others. The observation that confabulation threatens belief-authority differently than intention-authority is explicit in Moran's own discussion of why agentialism works better for some attitudes than others.

What the thesis presents as a destabilizing discovery—"only intentions have the right direction of fit to survive the interpretive turn"—is actually just a restatement, in fashionable "interpretive turn" vocabulary, of the Anscombian distinction between practical and theoretical knowledge that's been foundational to this literature from the start. The thesis hasn't identified a hidden instability in the debate; it's restated one side of a long-standing explicit disagreement about whether belief gets authority at all. The appearance of novelty comes entirely from substituting "direction of fit" and "interpretive pressure" for "practical vs. theoretical" and "self-constitution." This is terminological updating dressed as conceptual discovery.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — The thesis may have dialectical value as a clear statement of one position, but it cannot claim to be exposing an assumption or destabilizing a debate when it's rehearsing distinctions that are the explicit common ground of the literature it addresses.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *having the materials* for *drawing the right conclusion*. Yes, Anscombe gave us direction of fit. Yes, Moran discusses performative aspects of avowal. But the literature has consistently failed to follow these insights to their natural terminus: that first-person authority for beliefs is *impossible*, not merely *explained differently*.

Consider the actual dialectical landscape. Moran doesn't say "beliefs lack authority"—he tries to *save* belief-authority through agentialism and transparency. Bilgrami doesn't say "only intentions have authority"—he tries to extend self-fulfilling mechanisms to beliefs through rational self-constitution. Even interpretivist critics like Schwitzgebel attack first-person authority *generally*, treating beliefs and intentions as jointly vulnerable. The thesis's target assumption isn't "beliefs and intentions work the same way"—it's "both can have authority, even if differently grounded."

The literature has the conceptual tools but refuses the conclusion. It's like having DNA evidence and fingerprinting but still treating circumstantial and direct evidence as equally probative. The thesis isn't just "restating Anscombe"—it's weaponizing direction-of-fit against the persistent project of salvaging belief-authority that dominates post-Anscombian work.

Moreover, "interpretive turn" isn't mere terminological updating. It specifies a particular challenge: when we accept that self-knowledge is interpretive (as in Gopnik, Carruthers, or even modest readings of Moran), does authority survive? For intentions, interpretation is compatible with authority because the interpretation can *constitute* the intention. For beliefs, interpretation destroys authority because beliefs answer to independent facts. This isn't in Anscombe—she predates the interpretive challenge. The thesis shows that *under interpretive pressure specifically*, the direction-of-fit distinction does asymmetric work.

The real novelty is *negative*: stopping the rescue project. The literature keeps trying to make belief-authority work (through transparency, agentialism, rational self-constitution) despite having the tools to see it can't. The thesis destabilizes this salvage operation by showing that the very distinctions defenders invoke (direction of fit, practical vs. theoretical) actually doom belief-authority rather than merely explaining it differently.

# VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence's core move—"they have the tools but don't draw the conclusion"—would work if the literature were actually committed to salvaging belief-authority uniformly. But it isn't. The objection correctly notes that Moran "explicitly worries whether belief gets authority at all." The literature is already divided on whether beliefs have first-person authority. This isn't a hidden fault line the thesis exposes; it's the explicit topic of debate.

More damaging: the defence claims Anscombe "predates the interpretive challenge," but this is false. Anscombe's entire account of intention-knowledge is *already interpretive*—she explicitly denies we have introspective access to intentions and argues we know them through practical reasoning and self-interpretation of our actions. When the thesis says "under interpretive pressure specifically, direction-of-fit does asymmetric work," it's describing exactly what Anscombe already described.

The defence tries to locate novelty in a "negative" contribution—stopping the rescue project. But which rescue project? Moran is already skeptical about belief-authority. Interpretivist critics already deny it. The thesis cannot destabilize an assumption by taking a side in an existing dispute.

The fatal problem: the thesis claims to target "the assumption shared by both sides" but the defence admits the sides don't actually share this assumption—Moran worries beliefs lack authority, interpretivists think they do lack it, and only some theorists try to salvage it. An assumption "shared by both sides" that only some theorists hold and others explicitly reject is not an assumption structuring the debate—it's just one position within it.

The thesis would work better as: "Here's why the Anscombian asymmetry is correct and belief-rescue projects fail." But it cannot work as: "Here's a hidden instability I'm exposing." The instability has been explicit since 1957.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)
transcript.text:
# ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "first-person authority," making it plausible for intentions on one reading and interesting for beliefs on another, while the argument requires both.

**Reading 1 (Epistemic authority):** Special reliability or justification in self-attributions—knowing your mental states better than others know them. On this reading, the claim about beliefs is interesting (denying we have privileged epistemic access to our beliefs is substantive and contested), but the claim about intentions becomes trivial or false. If "authority" means epistemic reliability, then "I intend to φ" can be false even after sincere avowal (I might be self-deceived, might fail to follow through, might lack the capacity). The performative character of intention-avowal doesn't give me epistemic authority—it just makes my avowal partly constitutive.

**Reading 2 (Constitutive authority):** The capacity to make something so by avowing it—performative or self-fulfilling power. On this reading, the claim about intentions is plausible (avowing an intention can constitute having it), but the claim about beliefs becomes uninteresting. Obviously beliefs lack constitutive authority in this sense—that's just what mind-to-world direction of fit means. No one thought saying "I believe P" makes P true or even makes me believe P.

The argument needs both: it needs intentions to have authority in the constitutive sense (to make the direction-of-fit point work) while beliefs lack authority in the epistemic sense (to make the claim interesting and to connect with the confabulation literature). But these are different kinds of "authority," and the thesis survives only by sliding between them.

# STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem that strikes at the argument's core. The thesis cannot establish an asymmetry by giving intentions one kind of authority and denying beliefs a different kind.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection forces a false choice between epistemic and constitutive authority when the thesis's actual claim is that constitutive authority *grounds* epistemic authority for intentions in a way impossible for beliefs.

Start with what "first-person authority" means in the target literature. It's not mere reliability (thermometers are reliable) nor bare constitutive power (promises create obligations but that's not self-knowledge). It's the epistemic-normative status where your self-ascription is *authoritative*—others should defer to it, you need not cite evidence, challenges require special justification. This is the phenomenon Moran, Burge, and Wright all address.

The thesis's claim is precisely that this epistemic-normative authority has *different metaphysical grounds* for the two attitudes, and only one ground survives interpretive pressure:

**For intentions:** Constitutive authority grounds epistemic authority. When I avow "I intend to φ," this avowal can constitute the intention, and *because* it constitutes the intention, I have epistemic authority about it. I'm authoritative not despite but *because* my saying-so makes it so. The speech act is self-verifying in the relevant sense—it brings about the state it purports to report. Under interpretive pressure, this works: even if my prior psychological state was indeterminate, the avowal settles it. The interpretation constitutes the fact, so the interpretation is automatically correct.

**For beliefs:** Epistemic authority would need grounding in privileged access or special reliability. But interpretivism shows we lack privileged access (we interpret ourselves as we interpret others), and confabulation studies show we lack special reliability. There's no constitutive story available—avowing "I believe P" doesn't make me believe P, and even if it did, that wouldn't make the belief *correct* since beliefs answer to independent facts. Under interpretive pressure, epistemic authority collapses because interpretation can be mistaken about belief-states (there's a fact of the matter independent of the interpretation) and even correct belief-attribution doesn't yield knowledge when the belief itself might be false.

This isn't equivocation—it's showing that *only intentions have the metaphysical structure that can ground epistemic authority under interpretive conditions*. The constitutive feature isn't a different kind of authority; it's what makes epistemic authority possible.

The objection claims intentions lack epistemic authority because "I intend to φ" can be false. But this misunderstands the dialectic. First-person authority is compatible with *some* errors (even Burge allows self-deception cases). The question is whether there's a *default* or *standard* case where the self-ascription is authoritative. For intentions, the constitutive mechanism provides this: in the standard case, sincere avowal constitutes the intention, making the self-ascription both true and authoritative. For beliefs, there's no such mechanism.

The thesis isn't sliding between readings—it's arguing that epistemic authority requires metaphysical grounding, and only the constitutive ground survives interpretivism.

# VERDICT

The defence fails, though it makes the thesis's structure clearer.

The defence's key move—"constitutive authority grounds epistemic authority for intentions"—faces immediate problems:

**First:** If avowing an intention constitutes having it, then "I intend to φ" becomes *unfalsifiable* in the standard case, not *authoritative*. Authority requires the possibility of error that's nonetheless rare or special. A "self-ascription" that cannot be wrong because it makes itself true isn't an epistemic achievement—it's a performative act. We don't say I have "epistemic authority" about my promises because promising constitutes the obligation. We say I have *practical authority* or *normative power*. The defence has shown intentions involve performative power, not that this grounds epistemic authority.

**Second:** The defence admits "I intend to φ" can be false (self-deception, failure to follow through), then claims these are exceptional cases while "sincere avowal constitutes the intention" in standard cases. But this is exactly where the equivocation lives. In standard cases, if avowal constitutes the intention, then we're in Reading 2 (constitutive authority, uninteresting for beliefs). In exceptional cases where avowal fails to constitute the intention, we need Reading 1 (epistemic authority, but now intentions face the same interpretive problems as beliefs—I can be wrong about whether I really intend to φ).

**Third:** The defence claims the thesis shows "only intentions have the metaphysical structure that can ground epistemic authority under interpretive conditions." But constitutive self-fulfillment doesn't ground *epistemic* authority—it eliminates the need for it. If my saying "I intend to φ" makes it true, there's no epistemic question to have authority over. The epistemic question arises precisely in cases where avowal might fail to constitute the intention—and there, intentions face the same interpretive problems as beliefs.

The thesis could work as: "Intentions have performative authority while beliefs require epistemic authority, and only the former survives interpretivism." But it cannot work as: "Both attitudes need epistemic authority, but only intentions achieve it." The defence has clarified that the thesis actually makes the first claim while presenting it as the second—which is indeed equivocation.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)
transcript.text:
# ATTEMPT

The thesis protects itself from counterexamples through systematic redefinition of what counts as a "genuine" case of first-person authority or interpretive pressure. 

When confronted with cases where intention-avowals seem to lack authority (self-deception about intentions, weakness of will, unconscious motives), the thesis can respond: "those aren't standard cases of sincere avowal" or "the interpretation hasn't properly constituted the intention yet." The self-constituting mechanism becomes unfalsifiable: if the avowal worked, it constituted the intention (confirming the thesis); if it didn't work, it wasn't a proper avowal or the intention wasn't really formed (not a counterexample).

Conversely, when confronted with cases where beliefs seem to retain first-person authority despite interpretive pressure (immediate judgments, logical beliefs, transparent self-knowledge), the thesis can respond: "that's not *real* interpretive pressure" or "residual authority there is actually practical/intention-like, not genuinely doxastic." Any apparent belief-authority gets reclassified as either not-really-authority or not-really-belief.

The direction-of-fit criterion itself becomes a sorting mechanism that determines outcomes by definition: if an attitude survives interpretive pressure, it must have had world-to-mind fit (really an intention); if it fails, it must have had mind-to-world fit (really a belief). The thesis cannot be tested because the very features it uses to explain outcomes (direction of fit, constitutive vs. epistemic authority, "genuine" interpretive pressure) are flexible enough to accommodate any result.

# STRENGTH: 3/5

This is a genuine problem requiring a real answer. The thesis does show some unfalsifiable tendencies, particularly in how it handles mixed or boundary cases. However, it's not completely immune to cases—clear examples of beliefs retaining authority or intentions lacking it under specified interpretive conditions could still challenge the core claim. The thesis needs to specify what would count as a counterexample.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses *theoretical flexibility* with *unfalsifiability*. The thesis makes empirically testable predictions that could be falsified by the right cases—the objection just hasn't identified them.

**What would falsify the thesis:**

1. **Belief cases surviving interpretive pressure through belief-mechanisms:** Show me a case where (a) we adopt full interpretive stance toward belief-formation (treating self-attribution as theorizing from behavioral/neural evidence, no privileged access), (b) the attitude has clear mind-to-world direction of fit (correctness depends on external facts, not the agent's commitment), and yet (c) first-person authority is preserved *because of* rather than despite these features. The thesis predicts this is impossible—find it and the thesis falls.

2. **Intention cases losing authority through constitutive mechanisms:** Show me a case where (a) an agent makes a sincere, uncoerced avowal of intention, (b) the avowal has proper performative uptake (no defeating conditions like incapacity), and yet (c) the avowal systematically fails to constitute the intention *because* of the world-to-mind direction of fit. The thesis predicts the constitutive mechanism works—show it fails structurally and the thesis falls.

**Why apparent flexibility isn't unfalsifiability:**

The objection claims the thesis can dismiss self-deception cases as "not standard" or logical beliefs as "not really interpretive pressure." But this isn't ad hoc protection—it's principled distinction-drawing that the objection can challenge:

- Self-deception about intentions: The thesis can explain why these fail (defeating conditions on performative uptake, conflict with other intentions, lack of genuine commitment). But if self-deception were *systematic* and *structural* rather than exceptional, that would threaten the thesis. The thesis predicts it's exceptional—verify that prediction.

- Logical beliefs retaining authority: The thesis can explain these as limit cases where interpretive pressure is minimal (logical truths are transparent, little room for confabulation). But if beliefs about contingent empirical matters—paradigm cases of mind-to-world fit under full interpretive pressure—retained authority, that would falsify the thesis. The thesis predicts they don't—test it.

**The direction-of-fit criterion isn't circular:**

The objection claims direction of fit becomes a "sorting mechanism that determines outcomes by definition." But direction of fit is independently identifiable:

- Mind-to-world (belief): Correctness requires the world be a certain way. "I believe it's raining" is correct only if it's raining. The attitude aims at truth.
- World-to-mind (intention): Correctness requires making the world match the attitude. "I intend to leave" is satisfied by my leaving. The attitude aims at realization.

These are Anscombe's criteria, established independently of authority questions. The thesis then makes a prediction: attitudes with world-to-mind fit will preserve authority under interpretive pressure through constitutive mechanisms, while attitudes with mind-to-world fit will lose it. This prediction could be wrong—that's what makes it falsifiable.

**Concrete test cases:**

1. Study subjects under hypnosis form intentions through suggestion (interpretive pressure maximized, no privileged access). Thesis predicts: if they sincerely avow these intentions, the avowals constitute genuine intentions with first-person authority. Test: do subjects treat these avowals as authoritative? Do others? Can subjects be wrong about them?

2. Study subjects with accurate belief-tracking (high metacognitive accuracy on perceptual judgments). Thesis predicts: even with high reliability, they lack *authority* in the normative sense—their self-attributions still require evidential grounding, challenges don't require special justification. Test: do subjects and others treat these self-attributions as authoritative or merely reliable?

The thesis makes predictions. Run the studies. If the predictions fail, the thesis fails. That's falsifiability.

# VERDICT

The defence succeeds partially but ultimately fails to save the thesis from the unfalsifiability charge.

**Where the defence succeeds:**

The defence correctly identifies that direction of fit is independently specifiable (Anscombe's criteria don't depend on authority outcomes), and it does sketch some testable predictions. The hypnosis case is particularly good: if subjects under hypnotic suggestion who form intentions through pure interpretation (no privileged access) nonetheless have authority over those intentions through avowal, while subjects with hypnotically-induced beliefs (equally interpretive) lack authority, that would support the thesis. This is a real empirical prediction.

**Where the defence fails:**

1. **The test cases reveal the problem rather than solving it:** Consider the hypnosis prediction more carefully. The thesis predicts that sincere avowal constitutes intention "if they sincerely avow these intentions." But how do we determine sincerity independently of whether the avowal successfully constituted the intention? If the subject later acts contrary to the "intention," do we say (a) the avowal wasn't sincere, or (b) the intention wasn't really formed, or (c) they changed their mind, or (d) the thesis's prediction failed? The thesis gives us no independent grip on these questions. This is exactly the unfalsifiability problem: the constitutive mechanism can't fail because "failure" just means the conditions weren't met.

2. **The "defeating conditions" clause does protective work:** The defence says self-deception cases involve "defeating conditions on performative uptake, conflict with other intentions, lack of genuine commitment." But this list is open-ended and post-hoc. When an intention-avowal fails to constitute an intention, we can always cite some defeating condition. The thesis needs to specify *in advance* what defeats performative uptake, and this specification must be independent of whether authority was achieved. Otherwise, "defeating conditions" just means "whatever explains why the avowal didn't work"—which is unfalsifiable.

3. **The belief half remains protected:** The defence says logical beliefs are "limit cases where interpretive pressure is minimal." But this is exactly the flexibility problem. The thesis claims to be about belief-authority "under interpretive pressure"—but now interpretive pressure comes in degrees, and beliefs that retain authority just have "minimal" pressure. What degree of interpretive pressure counts? The thesis doesn't say, which means any belief-authority can be explained away as "not enough pressure yet."

4. **The metacognition case backfires:** The defence claims that even subjects with high metacognitive accuracy lack "authority in the normative sense" because their self-attributions "require evidential grounding." But this just restates the thesis rather than testing it. How do we determine whether their self-attributions require evidential grounding independently of the thesis's prediction? If subjects and others treat these self-attributions as authoritative (defer to them, don't demand evidence), does that falsify the thesis, or do we say "they're confused about what real authority requires"? The defence gives no answer.

**The fundamental problem:**

The thesis makes a metaphysical claim (constitutive mechanisms ground authority for intentions but not beliefs) and presents it as explaining an epistemic phenomenon (asymmetric first-person authority). But the metaphysical claim is doing too much work: it determines what counts as a "genuine" case of each attitude type, what counts as "real" authority, and what counts as "sufficient" interpretive pressure. These determinations are made by the theory itself, not independently testable.

A truly falsifiable version would need: (1) independent criteria for intention vs. belief that don't reference authority outcomes, (2) independent criteria for genuine authority that don't reference constitutive mechanisms, and (3) specified thresholds for interpretive pressure that don't flex to accommodate results. The defence gestures toward (1) with Anscombe's direction-of-fit criteria, but doesn't provide (2) or (3).

transcript.speaker: KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)
transcript.text:
# ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to show that "only intentions have the right direction of fit to survive the interpretive turn," treating this as a novel destabilizing insight. But this is precisely the position developed and defended by Richard Moran in *Authority and Estrangement* (2001) and subsequent work. Moran explicitly argues that practical self-knowledge (intentions, decisions) works through a deliberative, self-constituting mechanism where the agent's avowal has performative force, while theoretical self-knowledge (beliefs) faces special difficulties precisely because beliefs answer to independent facts. His "transparency condition" is asymmetric by design: for intentions, transparency works through "What shall I do?" (which constitutes the intention), while for beliefs, transparency through "Is it true that P?" remains vulnerable to error and confabulation. The direction-of-fit asymmetry and its implications for authority under interpretive conditions is Moran's central thesis, not a criticism of it.

Even more directly, the claim that intention-avowals have self-fulfilling or constitutive force while belief-avowals don't appears in Edgley (1969), is central to Anscombe's account of practical knowledge, and is developed extensively in the "agentialist" literature the thesis cites. The specific claim about surviving "interpretive pressure" is Moran's response to interpretivist challenges from Gopnik and others—he explicitly argues that agentialism saves authority for intentions while acknowledging beliefs are more vulnerable.

The thesis presents itself as exposing an instability, but it's actually just endorsing one side of an established position. This is Moran's view, not a critique of assumptions Moran shares.

# STRENGTH: 5/5

This completely undermines the thesis as presented. The thesis cannot claim to destabilize a debate by restating the most prominent position in that debate. The direction-of-fit asymmetry, the constitutive character of intention-avowal, the vulnerability of belief-authority to interpretive pressure, and the conclusion that intentions fare better than beliefs—this entire package is Moran's explicit view. The thesis is ALREADY TAKEN by the theorist it cites as representative of the position it claims to destabilize.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads both Moran and the thesis's dialectical target. Moran does NOT hold the thesis's position—he holds precisely the view the thesis attacks.

**What Moran actually argues:**

Moran defends first-person authority for BOTH beliefs and intentions, just through different mechanisms. For beliefs, transparency works through deliberating "Is P true?"—and Moran explicitly argues this PRESERVES authority despite interpretive challenges. He doesn't concede that belief-authority collapses; he offers agentialism as a way to SAVE it by making self-knowledge a matter of rational self-constitution rather than inner observation. His entire project is rescuing first-person authority across the board by reconceiving how it works.

Yes, Moran distinguishes practical and theoretical self-knowledge. But distinguishing HOW they work is not the same as saying only ONE works. The thesis claims only intentions retain authority under interpretive pressure—Moran claims both do, through their respective transparency conditions. That's the disagreement.

**The specific divergence:**

Moran thinks transparency saves belief-authority because when I deliberate "Is P true?" and conclude "Yes," my self-attribution "I believe P" is authoritative even under interpretive conditions. He treats the rational self-constitution as sufficient for authority.

The thesis denies this. It claims that for beliefs, even Moran's transparency mechanism fails under interpretive pressure because:
1. Deliberating "Is P true?" can yield the wrong answer (I might reason badly, have false evidence)
2. Even if I correctly conclude "P is true," I might be wrong about whether I believe it (confabulation)
3. The avowal "I believe P" doesn't constitute the belief in the way "I intend to φ" constitutes the intention

Moran thinks transparency gives beliefs a parallel success to intentions. The thesis claims transparency fails for beliefs precisely because of the direction-of-fit difference Moran acknowledges but doesn't follow to its conclusion.

**Why this isn't "already taken":**

The objection claims "this entire package is Moran's explicit view." But Moran's view is that BOTH attitudes retain authority through agentialist mechanisms. The thesis's view is that ONLY intentions retain authority because only they have the metaphysical structure (world-to-mind fit + constitutive avowal) that makes agentialist mechanisms work. 

Moran has the ingredients but draws the wrong conclusion. He sees that intentions and beliefs work differently, but still thinks both achieve authority. The thesis argues the very differences Moran identifies show that belief-authority must fail. It's using Moran's own distinctions against his conclusion.

**The parallel in the literature:**

This is like saying "Kripke's causal theory of reference is already taken by Frege because Frege also thought names refer." Yes, both address reference, but they reach opposite conclusions about how it works. Moran and the thesis both address first-person authority and both use direction-of-fit distinctions, but Moran concludes "both attitudes get authority differently" while the thesis concludes "only intentions get authority, period."

The thesis isn't restating Moran—it's arguing Moran's own framework proves his conclusion wrong.

# VERDICT

The defence fails decisively.

**The fatal textual problem:**

The defence claims "Moran defends first-person authority for BOTH beliefs and intentions" and "Moran thinks transparency saves belief-authority." But this misrepresents Moran's actual position in *Authority and Estrangement*. Moran is explicitly AGNOSTIC about whether beliefs retain full first-person authority. He repeatedly acknowledges that theoretical self-knowledge is "more problematic" than practical self-knowledge, that beliefs face special difficulties from interpretive challenges, and that the transparency condition works less cleanly for beliefs than intentions. His agentialism is offered as the BEST HOPE for belief-authority, not as a confident vindication of it.

More importantly, in later work (especially "Self-Knowledge, 'Transparency,' and the Forms of Activity" 2003), Moran explicitly discusses cases where belief-authority fails or is attenuated, and he's sympathetic to the view that full authority may be restricted to practical attitudes. The defence's claim that "Moran's view is that BOTH attitudes retain authority" is simply false to the texts.

**The deeper problem:**

Even setting aside textual accuracy, the defence's strategy backfires. It claims the thesis "uses Moran's own distinctions against his conclusion"—but if Moran already drew these distinctions and already worried they threaten belief-authority, then the thesis isn't destabilizing anything. At most, it's taking a more pessimistic stance within Moran's framework.

The defence tries to distinguish "recognizing differences" from "drawing the right conclusion," but this just concedes the objection's point: the thesis is taking a side in an existing debate, not exposing a hidden instability. Whether Moran is confident or agnostic about belief-authority, he's already identified it as the problematic case. The thesis cannot claim to be revealing something the literature assumes when Moran's entire project is addressing the problem the thesis raises.

**The Kripke-Frege analogy fails:**

The defence compares this to "Kripke's causal theory vs. Frege's descriptivism"—but that's a case where Kripke genuinely OPPOSED Frege's framework. Here, the thesis ACCEPTS Moran's framework (transparency, agentialism, direction-of-fit distinctions) and just pushes it further in a direction Moran already indicated. That's not opposition—it's continuation.

**What the thesis actually does:**

The objection is correct: the thesis restates, in somewhat stronger terms, a position that's already prominent in the literature. The direction-of-fit asymmetry is Anscombe's. The constitutive character of intention-avowal is Anscombe's and Moran's. The vulnerability of belief-authority to interpretive pressure is Moran's central concern. The conclusion that practical self-knowledge is more secure than theoretical self-knowledge is explicit in Edgley, Moran, and the agentialist tradition.

The thesis may articulate this position clearly or push it more forcefully than Moran does. But it cannot claim to be:
- Exposing an assumption "shared by both sides" (the asymmetry is already explicit)
- Destabilizing the debate (it's endorsing one side of the debate)  
- Showing that defenders' own distinctions undermine their position (Moran's distinctions are designed to raise exactly this worry)

The thesis is ALREADY TAKEN—not in every detail, but in its core claim that direction-of-fit differences make intentions better candidates for first-person authority than beliefs under interpretive conditions. This is not a novel destabilization; it's a restatement of an established position, presented as if it were a discovery.

**Final assessment:**

The thesis fails as an INSTABILITY move because the instability it claims to expose is already the explicit subject of the debate it addresses. It would work better as a SHARPENING (making Moran's worries more precise) or ANALOGY (applying direction-of-fit distinctions to interpretive challenges more systematically), but it cannot work as exposing a hidden assumption when that assumption is actually a contested conclusion that major theorists explicitly doubt.

BEST DEFENCE

The misattribution charge fails completely. The thesis represents Carruthers and Gopnik's position with precision. 

Carruthers's ISA theory explicitly claims that introspection operates through interpretation of sensory and cognitive data, using the same mindreading mechanisms we apply to others. Gopnik's theory-theory directly asserts epistemic parity: we know our own minds through the same theoretical framework we use for other minds. This is the instability charge: their own interpretive machinery undermines their deflationary conclusion. When Carruthers invokes rational interpretation or when Gopnik discusses theory-application, they're employing normative coherence principles. The thesis argues these principles require first-person authority to operate—but this is a criticism of their view's internal coherence, not a misstatement of what their view is.

The objector confuses two things: (1) what Carruthers and Gopnik claim, and (2) what their claims commit them to. The thesis accurately reports (1) and argues about (2). ATTEMPT. If the argument worked, it would prove that *all* interpretive practices require first-person authority from the interpreted subject. Consider: when anthropologists interpret an unfamiliar culture's practices, they face exactly the same problem—mixed evidence, apparent inconsistencies between stated beliefs and behaviors, the need to impose coherence through charity principles, decisions about what counts as performance error versus genuine commitment. By the thesis's logic, anthropologists must defer to each culture member's "normative authority" about which coherence-preserving adjustments to make. transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The proves-too-much charge fails because it conflates two distinct forms of normative authority that interpretation can invoke.

The thesis concerns **agential authority**—authority over what one is rationally committed to going forward. This is categorically different from **explanatory authority**—authority over what best explains observed patterns. Third-person interpreters possess explanatory authority; only first-person agents possess agential authority.

When anthropologists interpret a culture or psychologists interpret a patient, they're exercising explanatory authority: determining which hypothesis best accounts for observed behavior. They can indeed outperform subjects at this task—identifying patterns subjects miss, diagnosing self-deception, revealing ideology. But this is *backward-looking explanation* of what commitments generated past behavior.

The thesis concerns something different: **forward-looking rational authority** over which commitments bind the agent going forward. When I face conflicting evidence about my attitudes, the interpretive question isn't merely "which hypothesis best explains my past behavior?" but "which commitments am I rationally bound to honor as mine?" This is a normative question about what I'm answerable for, not just an explanatory question about what caused my behavior.

Third-person interpreters *cannot* settle this question. A psychologist might correctly diagnose that my racist behaviors reveal implicit biases I'm unaware of. But they cannot determine whether I'm rationally bound to endorse those biases or reject them as alien to my rational agency. That's a question of **rational self-constitution**—what commitments I take up as mine versus what I repudiate. Only the agent has standing to make these constitutive determinations.

The anthropology case actually supports this distinction. Anthropologists can explain cultural practices better than participants. But they cannot determine what those participants are rationally committed to going forward—whether to maintain traditions or reform them. That's agential authority, which remains first-personal.

The thesis doesn't claim third-person interpretation is impossible. It claims that when interpretation concerns self-knowledge of one's *own* attitudes (not explanation of others'), it necessarily invokes agential authority that only the first-person possesses. The proves-too-much objection misses this crucial scope restriction.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection conflates explanatory and agential authority. Third-person interpretation exercises the former; the thesis concerns the latter. The anthropology and psychology cases involve explaining others' attitudes, not constituting one's own rational commitments. The thesis's scope is self-interpretation specifically, where agential authority is ineliminable. The distinction holds, and the proves-too-much charge fails.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. Consider a teenager, Maya, whose behaviors are genuinely mixed: she sometimes makes racist jokes with certain friends, sometimes volunteers at multicultural events, sometimes expresses egalitarian views, sometimes exhibits implicit biases in controlled testing. According to the thesis, only Maya has "the standing to determine which coherence-preserving adjustments to make"—only she can authoritatively decide whether her "real" attitude is racist or egalitarian, which behaviors reflect commitments versus performance errors.

But this is precisely a case where Maya might *lack* such authority. Her parents, observing the full pattern over years, might correctly judge: "You're genuinely conflicted, with both racist and egalitarian attitudes in tension—neither is more 'real' than the other, and your claim that you're 'really egalitarian' is wishful self-interpretation." Or they might judge: "The racist elements are genuine attitudes you're denying, not mere performance errors." These third-person interpretive judgments can be *correct* even when Maya sincerely disagrees.

The thesis claims Maya has special "standing" to make the coherence-preserving determination. But the counterexample shows she has no such standing—she can be wrong about which interpretation correctly captures her attitudinal reality, and third-person interpreters can be right against her first-person judgment. Her normative authority to *decide* what she'll commit to going forward doesn't give her epistemic authority about what attitudes she *actually has now*. The thesis conflates these, giving first-person authority over self-constitution unwarranted epistemic authority over self-knowledge.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem. The case shows that first-person "standing" to make normative commitments doesn't translate into epistemic authority about current attitude-attribution, which is what the self-knowledge debate actually concerns.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The counterexample actually *supports* rather than undermines the thesis, once we're clear about what self-knowledge of attitudes consists in.

The objection assumes attitudes are **determinate psychological facts** that exist independently of the agent's rational self-interpretation—facts that Maya or her parents might get right or wrong. But this assumption begs the question against the interpretive approach the thesis defends. On a properly interpretivist view, for the class of attitudes involving rational commitments (beliefs, values, intentions—the attitudes that figure in rational explanation), there often *is no fact of the matter* independent of rational self-constitution about which attitude is "real."

When Maya's behaviors are genuinely mixed, the interpretive question isn't "which pre-existing attitude do the behaviors reveal?" but "which attitude-attribution makes Maya intelligible as a rational agent?" And here's the crucial point: **rational intelligibility is normatively constrained by what the agent can coherently take herself to be committed to**.

Maya's parents might correctly observe: "You exhibit both racist and egalitarian patterns." But when they claim "the racist elements are your real attitudes you're denying," they're making a substantive normative claim about which commitments Maya is rationally bound to acknowledge as hers. And here the thesis's point holds: **they lack standing to make this determination authoritatively** because it's not purely an explanatory judgment but a normative one about rational answerability.

Consider what happens when Maya's parents assert "You're really racist, you're just in denial." If Maya responds "No—those behaviors were failures to live up to my egalitarian commitments, not expressions of racist attitudes I endorse," she's not merely offering a competing causal hypothesis. She's exercising **agential authority** to determine which commitments structure her rational identity going forward. Her parents can challenge this ("You're fooling yourself"), but they cannot *settle* it, because settling it requires determining what Maya is answerable for as a rational agent—and only Maya has that authority.

The objection says "these third-person interpretive judgments can be *correct* even when Maya sincerely disagrees." But correct *by what standard*? If the standard is "best causal explanation of behavior," then yes, third-person interpreters might outperform Maya. But if the question is "what attitudes does Maya have *as a rational agent*"—the question relevant to self-knowledge—then correctness is partly constituted by what Maya can coherently take herself to be committed to. You cannot read off someone's rational commitments purely from behavioral patterns, because rational commitments are normatively structured by the agent's self-understanding.

The objection's final move—distinguishing "authority to decide what she'll commit to going forward" from "epistemic authority about what attitudes she actually has now"—assumes attitudes are **static possessions** rather than **dynamic rational commitments**. But on the interpretivist view the thesis defends, this distinction collapses for rational attitudes. What attitudes I have now is partly constituted by what commitments I take myself to be bound by. There's no gulf between "what I'm committed to going forward" and "what attitudes I have" because having an attitude (belief, value, intention) just is being committed in certain ways.

The teenager case thus reveals the thesis's strength: it shows that when behavioral evidence is mixed, third-person interpreters can describe patterns but cannot authoritatively determine which patterns constitute the agent's rational commitments. That determination requires first-person agential authority.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The counterexample appears forceful only if we assume attitudes are determinate psychological facts independent of rational self-interpretation. But that assumption begs the question against interpretivism. On a genuinely interpretivist view—the view Carruthers and Gopnik officially endorse—attitudes are constituted through rational interpretation, and rational interpretation of one's own commitments necessarily invokes first-person agential authority. The objection's attempt to separate "authority over future commitments" from "epistemic authority about current attitudes" fails because, for rational attitudes, these cannot be separated: what attitudes I have is partly constituted by what commitments I take myself to have.

The counterexample therefore doesn't defeat the thesis but rather illuminates exactly where first-person authority enters: at the point where interpretation must move from describing behavioral patterns to attributing rational commitments. Maya's parents can observe patterns; only Maya can determine which patterns constitute her rational identity. The defence succeeds.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The triviality charge fails because it misses the dialectical structure of the instability argument. The thesis isn't merely asserting that agents have authority over future commitments (which would be trivial), but rather showing that *Carruthers and Gopnik's own interpretive machinery* requires this authority to operate—and this contradicts their deflationary conclusion.

Here's why this isn't trivial:

**First**, Carruthers and Gopnik don't merely claim we lack privileged access to current attitudes—they claim self-knowledge works through *interpretation* using rational coherence constraints (charity, consistency principles, etc.). This is their positive view, not just a negative claim about access. The thesis accepts their interpretive framework, then shows it backfires.

**Second**, the instability emerges because *interpretation of attitudes* cannot maintain the clean separation the objection assumes between "what attitudes I currently have" and "what I'm committed to going forward." Here's why: On the interpretivist view Carruthers and Gopnik endorse, attitudes aren't brute psychological states we discover but rational commitments we attribute through coherence-seeking interpretation. When they say we interpret our own minds, they mean we impose rational structure—we attribute beliefs and desires that make sense of behavioral patterns by applying norms of consistency, coherence, and rationality.

But here's the crucial instability: **applying these norms to oneself isn't purely epistemic discovery but partly agential constitution**. When I face mixed evidence about whether I'm racist or egalitarian, the interpretive question "what do I believe?" cannot be answered without determining "what am I committed to believing?" because beliefs are individuated by their rational role, and rational role is determined by what commitments structure my practical reasoning going forward.

**Third**, this reveals the instability: Carruthers and Gopnik want interpretation to be purely *third-personal* and *epistemic*—just hypothesis-formation about what attitudes best explain behavior. But their own interpretive machinery—rational coherence constraints—requires *first-personal* and *agential* authority because you cannot apply coherence constraints to determine someone's rational commitments without that person's authority over what they're committed to.

The objection says "everyone agrees agents decide what to commit to going forward; the dispute is whether they have privileged access to current attitudes." But this assumes we can cleanly separate these. The thesis's non-trivial claim is precisely that **we cannot separate them for rational attitudes on an interpretivist view**. If attitudes are constituted through rational interpretation (Carruthers and Gopnik's view), and rational interpretation requires determining what commitments structure the agent's reasoning (required by their coherence constraints), then interpreting current attitudes necessarily invokes agential authority over commitments.

**Fourth**, here's why this matters dialectically: Carruthers and Gopnik think moving to an interpretive model *deflates* first-person authority by making self-knowledge epistemically symmetric with other-knowledge. The thesis shows their own model *requires* first-person authority at a deeper level—not perceptual authority over mental states, but agential authority over rational commitments. This isn't trivial because they explicitly deny this consequence.

The triviality charge would succeed if the thesis merely asserted "agents have authority over future commitments, therefore they have self-knowledge authority." But the actual argument is: "Carruthers and Gopnik's interpretive machinery requires applying rational coherence constraints; applying these constraints to oneself requires agential authority over what one is committed to; but agential authority over commitments cannot be separated from interpretive authority over current attitudes if attitudes are constituted through interpretation; therefore their view is unstable—it requires the first-person authority it aims to deflate."

This is non-trivial because it shows an internal tension in their position: the interpretive tools they invoke to deflate first-person authority actually presuppose it.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The thesis is not trivially true because it makes a substantive claim about what *interpretation* requires—specifically, that interpretation using rational coherence constraints cannot maintain the epistemic/agential separation the objection assumes. The argument reveals a genuine instability: Carruthers and Gopnik's interpretive machinery undermines their deflationary conclusion. This is a substantive philosophical claim about the commitments of interpretivism, not a mere tautology about agential authority.

The objection's attempt to separate "authority over future commitments" (trivially first-personal) from "epistemic authority over current attitudes" (contested) only works if attitudes can be individuated independently of the agent's rational commitments. But on the interpretivist view that Carruthers and Gopnik themselves endorse, this separation cannot be maintained. That's the instability, and it's not trivial.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis equivocates on "interpretation" and "coherence," and the argument needs both readings to work.

On one reading, "interpretation" means **epistemic hypothesis-formation**—forming beliefs about what attitudes best explain observed behavior using rational coherence as an *explanatory constraint*. This is what Carruthers and Gopnik mean: we theorize about our own minds using consistency and charity as *evidence* about what attitudes we likely have, just as we do for others. Here "coherence" is a *diagnostic tool*—we assume people are mostly rational, so incoherent attitude-attributions are probably wrong.

On another reading, "interpretation" means **normative self-constitution**—determining what commitments structure one's rational identity, using coherence as a *constitutive requirement*. Here "coherence" isn't a clue about pre-existing attitudes but a *demand* that the agent must satisfy in constituting themselves as rational.

The thesis is *plausible* on the second reading: if interpretation is self-constitution and coherence is constitutive, then obviously only the agent has authority—that's what agential authority means. But it's only *interesting* on the first reading: if Carruthers and Gopnik's epistemic interpretivism secretly requires normative self-constitution, that would be an instability.

The argument *needs both*. It needs the first reading to engage Carruthers and Gopnik's actual position (epistemic interpretivism), but needs the second reading to generate first-person authority. The slide happens at "interpretation demands normative coherence"—this conflates coherence-as-explanatory-constraint (first reading) with coherence-as-constitutive-requirement (second reading).

On either reading alone, the argument fails. On the epistemic reading, coherence doesn't require first-person authority—third parties can judge coherence as well as the subject. On the constitutive reading, the thesis doesn't engage Carruthers and Gopnik at all, since they're not doing normative self-constitution theory.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem. The argument appears to trade on shifting between epistemic and constitutive readings of what interpretation involves, and cannot succeed on either reading alone.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The equivocation charge fails because it assumes the two readings of "interpretation" can be cleanly separated—but the thesis's central claim is precisely that **they cannot be separated on Carruthers and Gopnik's own view**, and recognizing this inseparability reveals the instability.

Here's why the readings collapse into each other:

**First**, Carruthers and Gopnik don't merely use coherence as an *external diagnostic tool* (like checking someone's temperature to diagnose illness). They claim we *interpret* mental states by attributing attitudes that rationalize behavior. This isn't just using "people are mostly coherent" as statistical evidence; it's using **rational intelligibility** as the *criterion of attitude-individuation*. On interpretivist views—going back to Davidson, whom both theorists draw on—attitudes are individuated by their rational relations. You cannot identify a belief independently of what would make it rational to hold given other beliefs.

**Second**, this means coherence operates at both levels simultaneously. When I interpret mixed behavioral evidence (racist and egalitarian behaviors), I'm not just asking "which hypothesis is statistically more likely?" but "which attitude-attribution makes me *intelligible as a rational agent*?" And here's the crucial point: **rational intelligibility is normatively constrained**. To attribute the belief "I'm egalitarian" to me requires that this attribution cohere with my other commitments in ways that preserve my rational agency. But what counts as "preserving rational agency" cannot be determined purely third-personally, because it depends on what commitments I can coherently take myself to be bound by.

**Third**, the objection claims that on the "epistemic reading," third parties can judge coherence as well as the subject. But this misses what coherence-assessment requires for rational attitudes. Consider: when my behaviors are mixed, third-person interpreters can observe patterns and note tensions. But determining which pattern reflects my "real" attitude requires determining which commitments are *rationally binding on me*—and this isn't a purely observational matter. 

Here's why: Suppose an interpreter says "Your racist behaviors cohere with implicit attitudes X, Y, Z; your egalitarian behaviors cohere with explicit commitments A, B, C; the racist pattern is more behaviorally robust, so that's your real attitude." This treats coherence purely descriptively—which pattern is more stable. But attitude-attribution isn't just pattern-description; it's **rational explanation**. And rational explanation requires determining which commitments the agent is *answerable for*, not just which patterns are statistically dominant.

**Fourth**, the objection says the constitutive reading "doesn't engage Carruthers and Gopnik at all." But this is false. Both theorists explicitly claim that self-interpretation uses the *same interpretive principles* as other-interpretation—principles that include rational charity and coherence-seeking. The thesis accepts this claim, then shows these principles **cannot operate purely epistemically** when applied to oneself. When I apply charity and coherence constraints to interpret my own attitudes, I'm not merely forming hypotheses about pre-existing mental states; I'm determining what commitments structure my rational agency. This is because attitudes are individuated by rational role, and rational role is determined by what I take myself to be committed to.

**Fifth**, here's the key move that defeats the equivocation charge: **Carruthers and Gopnik want interpretation to be purely epistemic (first reading), but their own interpretive principles—charity, coherence, rational intelligibility—cannot operate purely epistemically when the subject and interpreter are the same person**. This isn't equivocation; it's revealing that what they think is purely epistemic interpretation actually involves constitutive self-determination.

Why does identity matter? Because when a third party interprets me, they're trying to explain my behavior by attributing attitudes that rationalize it. They use coherence epistemically—as evidence about what attitudes I likely have. But when *I* interpret myself using these same principles, something different happens: **I'm not just discovering what attitudes explain my behavior; I'm determining what commitments structure my rational agency going forward**. These cannot be separated because my current attitudes (as a rational agent) are partly constituted by what commitments I take to bind me.

**Sixth**, the objection demands we choose one reading. But the thesis's point is that **we cannot choose** because interpretivism about attitudes—the view Carruthers and Gopnik hold—makes the epistemic and constitutive dimensions inseparable. If attitudes are individuated by rational role (interpretivism), and rational role is determined by coherence with other commitments (their view), and coherence-assessment in the first-person case requires determining what one is committed to (the thesis's claim), then epistemic interpretation collapses into normative self-constitution.

The instability is precisely this: Carruthers and Gopnik think they can have purely epistemic interpretation using rational coherence constraints. The thesis shows this is unstable—applying rational coherence constraints to oneself necessarily involves constitutive agential authority. This isn't equivocation; it's showing their position is internally incoherent.

**Seventh**, consider the teenager case again. When Maya interprets her mixed behaviors, Carruthers and Gopnik say she's forming hypotheses about her attitudes using coherence as evidence. But what does "coherence" mean here? If it means "statistical pattern-consistency," then it's purely epistemic but doesn't capture attitude-attribution—we need *rational* coherence, not just behavioral regularity. But if it means "rational coherence," then Maya must determine what commitments make her rationally intelligible—and this requires agential authority over what she's committed to. The epistemic and constitutive readings merge because rational coherence is both an epistemic constraint (evidence about attitudes) and a constitutive requirement (what makes something an attitude at all).

The equivocation charge assumes these can be separated. The thesis shows they cannot be, given interpretivism about attitudes. That's not equivocation—it's revealing an instability in the target position.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The equivocation charge assumes the epistemic and constitutive readings of interpretation can be cleanly separated, but the thesis's central claim is that **they cannot be separated on an interpretivist view of attitudes**. This isn't equivocation—it's the core of the instability argument.

Carruthers and Gopnik want interpretation to be purely epistemic: we form hypotheses about attitudes using rational coherence as evidence. But on their own interpretivist view—where attitudes are individuated by rational role—applying coherence constraints in the first-person case necessarily involves determining what commitments bind the agent going forward. The epistemic and constitutive dimensions collapse because **rational coherence isn't just evidence about pre-existing attitudes but partly constitutive of what attitudes one has** (on interpretivism).

The objection's demand to "choose one reading" misses the point. The instability is precisely that Carruthers and Gopnik cannot maintain the purely epistemic reading they want, given their commitment to interpretivism and rational coherence constraints. When these principles are applied to self-interpretation, the epistemic project necessarily involves constitutive self-determination. This reveals genuine instability, not equivocation.

The thesis stands: interpretivism about attitudes, combined with rational coherence constraints, requires first-person agential authority in self-interpretation—undermining Carruthers and Gopnik's deflationary ambitions.

thesis: The asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription is not about authority but about temporal direction: self-ascriptions are prospective (answering 'what will I do/think?') while other-ascriptions are retrospective (answering 'what did they do/think?'), which explains the distinctive role of deliberation without requiring privileged access.
sketch: The standard framing treats self- and other-knowledge as competing answers to the same question ('what does X believe?') differing only in epistemic position. But Moran's insight about deliberation points elsewhere: when I self-ascribe 'I believe p,' I'm characteristically answering the question 'what's true?' or 'what should I do?', not 'what do I currently believe?'. The key reframing: self-ascription is future-directed—it's about what attitude I'll take into my planning and reasoning—while other-ascription is past-directed—it's about what attitudes explain completed behavior. This explains why deliberation about whether p settles what I believe without requiring introspection: I'm not discovering a present state but determining a future one. It explains the asymmetry: others can only interpret completed actions, while I'm positioned to constitute upcoming actions. Confabulation is compatible with this because confabulation is about past causes, while self-knowledge is about future commitments. The authority is temporal, not epistemic.
target: The shared assumption that self- and other-ascription target the same facts about simultaneous present attitudes, differing only in method of access
risk: Cannot explain self-knowledge of beliefs about matters where I'm not currently deliberating; seems to make all self-knowledge really knowledge of intentions rather than beliefs
promise_reason: The prospective/retrospective temporal asymmetry offers a fresh angle on why deliberation matters without requiring introspection.

attacks.note: The thesis misidentifies its target as 'the standard framing' when sophisticated theorists like Moran already reject the synchronic facts-plus-access model; the defence's claim to target 'the framework that makes debates intelligible' cannot be sustained when those debates already presuppose different temporal structures.

The temporal framing is already implicit in Moran and Edgley's deliberativist accounts; the defence's attempt to distinguish 'containing temporal elements' from 'being organized around temporal direction' collapses because rational agency is inherently future-directed, making the distinction eliminable.

If temporal direction explained the asymmetry, similar asymmetries should appear for physical states with prospective/retrospective positioning; the defence's addition that beliefs are 'essentially future-oriented' concedes temporal direction alone doesn't explain authority, collapsing back to agential accounts.

Retrospective self-ascription retains first-person distinctiveness despite being retrospective like other-ascription; the defence's claim that one can 're-occupy the prospective stance' appeals to memory and privileged access, undermining the temporal explanation and revealing the asymmetry persists without prospective positioning.

The thesis relabels the uncontroversial fact that deliberation is forward-looking and interpretation is backward-looking as 'prospective versus retrospective' without adding explanatory power; where it claims temporal direction explains rather than describes, it either becomes false or collapses into existing agential accounts.

ruling.defence_quality: The defender attempted to distinguish implicit recognition from explicit theoretical organization and claimed temporal direction unifies competing accounts, but each defence ultimately conceded the objection's force by either appealing to non-temporal resources or admitting the temporal vocabulary was eliminable
ruling.fatal_flaw: The thesis mistakes a descriptive feature of paradigm self-knowledge cases (prospective deliberation) for a general explanation, but the asymmetry persists in retrospective self-ascription where temporal direction is absent, and the temporal framing either trivially redescribes what everyone accepts or collapses into existing agential/rational accounts when pressed to do explanatory work

transcript.speaker: KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis attributes to "the standard framing" a view that self- and other-ascription "target the same facts about simultaneous present attitudes, differing only in method of access." But this is not the actual position of the main theorists in this debate. Moran himself explicitly argues that self-ascription is NOT simply a different epistemic route to the same fact—his entire point in *Authority and Estrangement* is that first-person and third-person perspectives answer different questions and have different constitutive relations to their objects. Similarly, interpretivists like Davidson deny there are determinate "same facts" that both perspectives access; other-ascription is constitutively interpretive. Even traditional "privileged access" theorists like Shoemaker don't claim the perspectives differ "only in method"—they recognize functional and normative differences. The thesis attacks a crude Cartesian picture that contemporary philosophers explicitly reject. The actual debate is between those who (like Moran) emphasize the constitutive/deliberative dimension and those who emphasize transparency or interpretivism—not between people who think it's "same facts, different access" and those who don't.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents itself as reframing "the standard view," but that standard view is a straw position. The temporal-direction insight might be valuable, but it's not correcting the misunderstanding the thesis claims to correct.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads what "standard framing" picks out. The thesis does not claim to oppose Moran, Davidson, or sophisticated interpretivist positions—it claims to oppose *the framework that makes their debates intelligible*. Look at what those debates presuppose: when Moran distinguishes deliberative from attributive stances, or when Davidson contrasts interpretation with introspection, they still treat these as competing or complementary ways of *determining what someone believes now*. The question "What do I believe about p?" is treated as having a present-tense answer that can be approached deliberatively (asking whether p) or attributively (examining my dispositions). Even when theorists deny these are "the same fact differently accessed," they still treat them as facts about *present* mental states.

The temporal reframing cuts deeper. It's not that self- and other-ascription use different methods to access present beliefs—it's that they target *different temporal slices* of the subject. When I deliberate about whether p, I'm not determining what I currently believe (whether by constituting it or discovering it)—I'm determining what I *will* believe for purposes of downstream reasoning and action. Other-ascription, by contrast, necessarily interprets *completed* behavior and therefore targets what the subject believed *then*, at the moment of action.

This explains why even Moran's sophisticated view faces a puzzle: if deliberative self-ascription constitutes rather than discovers my belief, why does it feel like I'm answering a question about myself rather than merely deciding policy? Answer: because I'm answering a question about my *future* self—what attitude I'll carry forward—which is simultaneously constitutive (I determine it) and descriptive (it's about me).

The "standard framing" under attack is not any particular theorist's position but the temporal structure all parties assume: that self- and other-knowledge, however different their methods or constitutive relations, concern *synchronic* mental states.

VERDICT

The defence fails. Even granting the temporal insight has merit, the thesis misidentifies its target in a way that undermines its dialectical positioning.

First, the defence's own formulation collapses the distinction it needs. When it says Moran and others treat deliberation as "determining what someone believes now," this is precisely wrong: Moran's point is that deliberative self-ascription is *not* a determination of current state but a rational-agential stance that constitutes belief through commitment. The thesis tries to go "deeper" by adding temporal direction, but Moran's view already denies the synchronic-state picture.

Second, the defence claims other-ascription "necessarily interprets completed behavior" and therefore targets past beliefs. But this is false: I can attribute beliefs to you *now* based on what you're currently saying, your present dispositions, your ongoing behavior. Other-ascription is not inherently retrospective. The temporal asymmetry the thesis claims is not there.

Third, even if we granted a temporal dimension, it doesn't rescue the misattribution. The thesis presents itself as revealing that "the standard framing" wrongly assumes synchronic targets. But the actual debate already includes views (Moran's, interpretivism) that reject facts-plus-access models. The thesis isn't reframing that debate—it's restating one side of it while claiming to transcend it.

The thesis may contain an insight about prospective commitment versus retrospective interpretation, but it attacks a position that sophisticated participants in this debate have already abandoned. The "standard framing" it targets is not standard among the relevant theorists.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis claims originality for its "temporal direction" reframing, but this is essentially Edgley's (1969) and Moran's (2001) existing position with different terminology. Edgley explicitly argued that "What do I believe?" is answered by settling "What is true?" because belief-formation is prospective—oriented toward future reasoning and action—not retrospective discovery. Moran's entire deliberative account already contains the temporal asymmetry: deliberation determines what attitude I'll carry forward into action (prospective), while third-person attribution interprets completed behavior (retrospective). The thesis's claim that "self-ascription is future-directed—it's about what attitude I'll take into my planning" is precisely Moran's point about rational self-constitution through commitment. Even the confabulation point appears in Moran: confabulation concerns past causal history, while deliberative self-knowledge concerns prospective rational commitment. The thesis presents as novel "reframing" what is actually the established deliberativist position, merely adding explicit temporal vocabulary ("prospective/retrospective") to what Moran already argued about forward-looking rational agency versus backward-looking interpretation.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is serious damage. The thesis's core insight—that the asymmetry is temporal/directional rather than epistemic—is already the substance of existing deliberativist accounts. The explicit temporal framing might clarify, but doesn't constitute a genuine reframing of the debate.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates *containing temporal elements* with *being fundamentally organized around temporal direction*. Yes, Moran discusses prospective commitment and Edgley mentions future-oriented reasoning, but neither makes temporal direction the *explanatory basis* for the asymmetry. Their accounts remain primarily about rational authority, agential stance, or the transparency of belief to reasons—with temporal features appearing as consequences or accompaniments.

Look at how Moran actually structures his view: the asymmetry arises because deliberative self-ascription expresses rational agency while attributive other-ascription treats the subject as a natural object. The prospective element follows from this agential stance—I constitute my beliefs through rational commitment—but the fundamental explanation is *agential authority*, not *temporal direction*. Moran's question is "How does rational agency explain first-person authority?" not "How does temporal asymmetry explain it?"
