I display the same behavioral dispositions whether a belief is occurrent or merely standing; context doesn't reliably distinguish them. If interpretation is our only access, we cannot maintain that some beliefs are occurrent while others are merely dispositional—that distinction requires the kind of inner awareness interpretivists reject. Yet eliminativism about this distinction is deeply counterintuitive (surely there's a difference between currently thinking about P and merely being disposed to affirm it). Interpretivists face a forced choice: accept the counterintuitive eliminativism or grant some non-interpretive access.
target: Interpretivists like Carruthers who reject introspective access while maintaining standard belief-type distinctions
risk: Interpretivists might accept the eliminativism as a bullet worth biting, or might argue that different behavioral signatures do distinguish occurrent from dispositional states in ways interpretation can track
promise_reason: Interpretivism threatening the occurrent/dispositional distinction is a real problem but the issue is known.

thesis: The confabulation literature shows not that we lack first-person authority but that we systematically misidentify which mental states we have authority about: we have direct access to standing commitments but not to occurrent causation.
sketch: Nisbett and Wilson subjects confabulate about what caused their choice (an occurrent process), not about what they chose or intend going forward (a standing state). The literature conflates two things we might have authority about: the causal history of our mental states versus the normative commitments those states involve. First-person authority was always about the latter—I'm authoritative about what I believe, not about why I came to believe it. This distinction reclassifies the debate: interpretivists are right that we self-interpret causal processes, but this doesn't threaten authority over the rational commitments we undertake. The confabulation data actually presupposes subjects have authority about their choices/preferences (that's what they correctly report) while lacking it about psychological mechanisms.
target: Both sides' shared assumption that confabulation data undermines traditional authority wholesale, rather than delimiting its proper scope
risk: The distinction may be unstable if standing commitments are themselves individuated by their causal-historical properties, or if what we're committed to depends constitutively on how we got there
promise_reason: Useful distinction between causal and normative authority, but the move to save first-person authority by restricting its domain is fairly well-trodden.

thesis: Accepting the interpretive model commits you to denying the psychological reality of implicit attitudes, since the same evidence that makes implicit attitudes posits necessary makes first-person reports about explicit attitudes authoritative.
sketch: Interpretivists cite implicit attitudes as evidence we need interpretation to access our real attitudes. But implicit attitudes are posited precisely because they dissociate from what subjects sincerely avow. If we're interpretivists all the way down, we have no principled basis for treating IAT results as revealing 'real attitudes' that subjects are wrong about—they're just more behavioral data requiring interpretation. The interpretivist move requires treating some self-reports as authoritative (to create the contrast with implicit measures) while denying authority in general. Either sincere avowals have default authority—in which case implicit attitudes aren't attitudes at all but mere dispositions—or nothing has authority and implicit 'attitudes' are just patterns we choose to interpret as such. The key premise is that the implicit/explicit distinction requires asymmetric epistemic treatment that interpretivism cannot sustain.
target: Interpretivist positions (Carruthers, Gopnik) that use implicit attitude data as evidence for their view
risk: Interpretivists might accept the elimination of implicit attitudes as psychological kinds, treating them merely as behavioral patterns; or they might argue for a two-tier interpretivist account
promise_reason: The tension between interpretivism and implicit attitudes is real but extensively discussed.

thesis: The agentialist and neo-expressivist accounts are unstable because they require that deliberative reasons-responsiveness grounds authority, but being reasons-responsive requires accurate beliefs about what reasons one has, which returns us to the observational model they reject.
sketch: Moran grounds authority in the transparency method: I answer 'Do I believe P?' by answering 'Is P true?', taking a deliberative stance. Bar-On grounds it in expressive speech acts. Both require that the subject be appropriately responsive to reasons or can expressively manifest genuine attitudes. But this responsiveness requires that I can accurately tell what reasons I actually take to support what, or which attitudes I'm genuinely expressing. If I'm systematically wrong about my reasons (motivated reasoning) or express attitudes I don't have (confabulation), the agentialist move fails. To know I'm being appropriately reasons-responsive rather than rationalizing, I need the very observational access to my psychology that these views were meant to replace. The views collapse back into requiring inner perception of reasons-structures or genuine attitudes.
target: Moran's agentialism and Bar-On's neo-expressivism
risk: These views might respond that reasons-responsiveness is a normative status, not a psychological state requiring observation, or that expression is self-verifying in a way that blocks the regress
promise_reason: Valid internal criticism that agentialism requires what it rejects, but this circularity objection has been raised; competent but not groundbreaking.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved under interpretation because the self-ascriber has diachronic authority to make their past self interpretively consistent, a power third-person interpreters lack because they must treat the subject as a fixed explanatory target.
sketch: When I interpret myself as believing P based on my behavior, I can retroactively make this interpretation correct by committing now to P and treating my past actions as expressions of this commitment. Third-person interpreters cannot do this—they must take my psychology as whatever explains my behavior, not whatever I now decide it should be taken as. This creates an asymmetry: self-interpretation can be self-fulfilling across time in a way other-interpretation cannot. The power isn't epistemic access but diachronic rational control: I have authority because I can bring my past self into coherence with my current interpretation by undertaking commitments now. The key premise is that attitudes are individuated partly by diachronic rational relations that subjects can author but observers can only discover.
target: Interpretivists like Carruthers who assimilate self and other interpretation, and traditional observationalists who locate authority in synchronic access
risk: This may only explain authority about current attitudes formed through self-interpretation, not authority about what one believed before the interpretive act; it might also be too voluntaristic about belief
promise_reason: Diachronic authority to revise past self-interpretation is interesting but the temporal element has been explored.

thesis: First-person authority derives not from privileged access to mental states but from our constitutive role in settling which interpretations of our own ambiguous evidence count as correct.
sketch: The debate falsely assumes that either we observe determinate mental states (traditional view) or we interpret evidence that settles facts about us independently of our interpretation (Carruthers/Gopnik). But mental states are often genuinely indeterminate until we take a stance. When I wonder 'Do I really want to go to the party?', the behavioral and phenomenological evidence may radically underdetermine the answer. First-person authority isn't epistemic privilege about pre-existing facts, but practical authority to make certain interpretations true by adopting them. This explains the asymmetry: others can interpret my evidence, but only I can settle it by committing to an interpretation. The key premise is that for many attitudes, there's no fact of the matter independent of self-interpretation—we have interpretive sovereignty over indeterminate cases.
target: Both observationalists and interpretivists who assume mental states have determinate identity conditions independent of the subject's self-interpretation
risk: May only apply to a narrow range of attitudes (those genuinely indeterminate), leaving most cases unexplained, or collapse into a form of self-constitution that makes systematic error about one's attitudes impossible
promise_reason: Interpretive sovereignty over indeterminate attitudes is a known position; the formulation is clear but not novel.

thesis: The interpretive model actually vindicates rather than threatens first-person authority, because self-interpretation operates under rational constraints that other-interpretation does not—namely, requirements of agential coherence that make certain self-ascriptions rationally impermissible.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers assume that if self-knowledge is interpretive, then the asymmetry between first and third person collapses—we're just another interpreter of our own evidence. But this ignores that self-ascribing a belief or intention places it into a web of rational commitments that constrains future deliberation and action in ways that merely ascribing it to another does not. When I judge 'I believe P', I'm not just reporting; I'm taking responsibility for treating P as a premise in reasoning. This creates asymmetric rational pressure: certain self-interpretations become impermissible because they would make me incoherent as an agent, while no such constraint binds third-person interpretation. The key premise is that self-ascription is itself a rational act answerable to agential coherence requirements, not merely a descriptive judgment.
target: Interpretivists who think symmetric evidential access entails symmetric authority
risk: May merely relocate rather than explain the asymmetry—why does self-ascription carry these special rational commitments? Seems to presuppose rather than explain first-person authority
promise_reason: Rational constraints on self-interpretation creating asymmetry is interesting but the agential coherence requirement angle has been developed in the Moran-adjacent literature.

thesis: Anyone who accepts that we can have non-interpretive knowledge of our sensory experiences is committed to accepting non-interpretive knowledge of at least some attitudes, because the same cognitive architecture that delivers experiential awareness also delivers awareness of cognitive feelings (fluency, rightness, attraction) that partially constitute attitudes.
sketch: Even radical interpretivists typically grant direct access to phenomenal consciousness—what it's like to see red isn't something we infer. But recent cognitive science shows that attitudes come with characteristic cognitive phenomenology: feelings of fluency, coherence, rightness, attraction-to-propositions. These aren't mere accompaniments but partial constitutents of what makes something a belief rather than a supposition, or an intention rather than a fantasy. If you grant direct access to visual phenomenology, you're committed to granting it to cognitive phenomenology. And since these cognitive feelings partly constitute attitudes, we have non-interpretive access to attitudinal components. The interpretive work comes in integrating these feelings into full attitude ascriptions, not in accessing the feelings themselves. The key premise is that cognitive phenomenology is no less phenomenal than sensory phenomenology.
target: Interpretivists who accept experiential realism but deny introspective access to attitudes
risk: Cognitive phenomenology may be too subtle, inconsistent, or ambiguous to ground the kind of authority we associate with self-knowledge, or it may not exist at all in the robust sense required
promise_reason: Cognitive phenomenology argument is competent and the parity reasoning is valid, but this strategy is already deployed in debates about introspection of thought.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved on the interpretive model not because self-interpretation is epistemically superior but because it is pragmatically self-fulfilling: self-ascribing an attitude changes the evidence base in ways that make the self-ascription correct, while other-ascription lacks this performative power.
sketch: The debate assumes authority must be epistemic—about better access to pre-existing facts. But self-ascriptions of attitudes are performative: avowing 'I intend to quit smoking' doesn't just report an intention but strengthens it, making the utterance self-verifying in a way third-person ascriptions aren't. When I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation tends to ratify itself by focusing attention on P-supporting evidence, recruiting P as a premise in reasoning, etc. Not through bias but through the dynamic nature of attitudes themselves—they are partially constituted by self-conception. Other-interpreters can't produce this effect. Authority isn't about better tracking but about interpretive acts that alter what they purport to track. The key premise is that attitudes are dynamically responsive to self-interpretation in ways that make self-ascription reliable through self-fulfillment rather than through superior evidence.
target: Both sides of the debate who assume first-person authority must be explained epistemically rather than pragmatically
risk: This may explain reliability without explaining authority—self-fulfilling predictions are reliable but not authoritative. Also risks making all self-ascriptions trivially correct, eliminating the possibility of self-deception or error
promise_reason: Self-fulfilling self-ascription is interesting but overlaps significantly with thesis 5 and existing work on performative self-knowledge; incremental development.

thesis: First-person authority for attitudinal states is grounded not in privileged access to mental content but in constitutive authority over what counts as executing one's intentions and commitments, which creates asymmetry even when self-knowledge is fully interpretive.
sketch: The debate conflates two kinds of authority: epistemic authority (knowing what attitudes you have) and executive authority (making it the case that you have certain attitudes through uptake and commitment). When I avow an intention, I'm not merely reporting a pre-existing mental state but performing an act that constitutes commitment. This executive authority creates genuine first-person asymmetry because others cannot make my commitments for me, even if they interpret my psychology better than I do. The key premise is that some self-ascriptions are world-to-mind direction of fit performatives rather than mind-to-world reports, and this performative dimension survives even when the self-interpretation leading to the performative is no more privileged than third-person interpretation.
target: Both Carruthers/Gopnik (who assume interpretive symmetry means no authority) and Moran/Bar-On (who ground authority in special access rather than executive powers)
risk: May not extend beyond intentions to beliefs and other non-voluntary attitudes; executive authority might collapse into mere stipulation without tracking psychological reality
promise_reason: Executive versus epistemic authority distinction is useful, but the performative dimension of avowals is well-established in expressivist literature.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved under interpretivism because self-interpretation operates under a distinctive rational pressure—the pressure of existential coherence—that third-person interpretation lacks, making even interpretively-derived self-ascriptions non-accidentally reliable in a way other-ascriptions are not.
sketch: When I interpret myself, getting it wrong creates practical incoherence in my life (I pursue goals that don't reflect my values, make commitments I can't sustain), generating pressure to revise interpretation until reflective equilibrium is reached. Third-person interpreters face no such pressure; their false interpretations of me don't destabilize their own lives. This creates a structural asymmetry: self-interpretation is self-correcting through lived experience in a way other-interpretation isn't. The key premise is that accuracy in self-interpretation is not merely an epistemic good but a practical requirement for coherent agency, creating a feedback loop between interpretation and action that grounds a distinctive kind of reliability even when the interpretive method is the same.
target: Gopnik's argument that if the method is the same, the epistemic position must be symmetrical
risk: Pressure toward coherence might produce systematic self-deception rather than accuracy; practical coherence could be achieved through false but adaptive self-narratives
promise_reason: Existential coherence pressure creating self-correcting interpretation is plausible, but the practical feedback loop has been noted in agentialist accounts.

thesis: Moran's agentialism and Carruthers' interpretivism both fail because they assume transparency: Moran assumes attitudes are transparent to deliberation, Carruthers assumes behavior is transparent to interpretation, but attitudinal states are constitutively opaque—defined by counterfactual commitments that outrun any evidence available to any interpreter including oneself.
sketch: To believe that P is to be disposed to treat P as true across an open-ended range of counterfactual circumstances, including those you've never encountered and cannot anticipate. Neither deliberation (Moran's method) nor interpretation of actual behavior and context (Carruthers' method) can determine these counterfactual commitments because they extend beyond available evidence. This reveals an unnoticed commitment: both views assume that attitudinal states are the kind of thing that can be made fully determinate by some accessible method. The key premise is that beliefs and intentions are individuated by normative commitments that transcend their causal basis, making them constitutively underdetermined by any evidence. First-person authority is thus illusory not because interpretation is doing the work, but because there's no fact of the matter that any method could access.
target: The shared assumption across the debate that there is a determinate fact about what we believe/intend that either introspection or interpretation could in principle access
risk: Commits to an implausibly strong indeterminacy; everyday attributions of beliefs seem too successful for there to be no fact of the matter; may conflate semantic underdetermination with metaphysical indeterminacy
promise_reason: Counterfactual commitments outrunning evidence is a deep point but the underdetermination argument is familiar.

thesis: The asymmetry between self- and other-ascription is not about authority but about stakes: self-ascriptions inherit the practical stakes of the attitudes they ascribe (believing I'm racist has different stakes than believing you're racist), and this stakes-asymmetry masquerades as epistemic authority in the literature.
sketch: What philosophers have identified as first-person authority is actually first-person practical impact. When I ascribe racism to myself versus to you, the ascriptions have different action-guiding implications and identity-constitutive significance for me, making me more careful, more resistant, and more invested in getting my own case right. This looks like special epistemic access but is actually special practical significance triggering different evidential standards. The key premise is that we conflate 'asymmetry in how the ascription matters' with 'asymmetry in epistemic position.' On this view, Moran is right that self-ascription is tied to deliberation, but wrong that this reveals a distinctive epistemic method; it reveals distinctive practical stakes that make the same interpretive method operate differently in the first-person case.
target: Moran and Bar-On's claim that first-person/third-person asymmetry reflects a deep epistemic or metaphysical difference rather than a pragmatic one
risk: Stakes-asymmetry may presuppose rather than explain authority (why do self-ascriptions have different stakes unless we already have some authority over them?); doesn't explain cases where we defer to others about our own attitudes despite high stakes
promise_reason: Stakes-asymmetry masquerading as epistemic asymmetry is a useful deflationary move, but the practical versus epistemic distinction has been explored in related contexts.

thesis: First-person authority and interpretive models are compatible because confabulation itself exhibits a distinctive first-person asymmetry: we confabulate about our reasons but not about our commitments, and it is commitments, not reasons, that ground authority.
sketch: The confabulation literature is taken to undermine first-person authority wholesale, but this assumes authority concerns knowing why we hold attitudes (our reasons). Draw a distinction between reasons (the causal or justificatory basis for attitudes) and commitments (the normative stance we take by holding attitudes). Nisbett and Wilson show we confabulate about reasons; they don't show we're wrong about what we're committed to defending or living by. The key premise: first-person authority concerns whether I'm right that believing P commits me to Q, or that intending A is incompatible with intending B—structural, normative questions about my attitudinal economy, not causal-genetic questions about why I formed the attitudes. We can be interpretive about the latter while retaining authority about the former because we have practical authority over what follows from our commitments.
target: Schwitzgebel and others who use confabulation data to undermine first-person authority without distinguishing what kind of self-knowledge is compromised
risk: The reasons/commitments distinction might not be sharp enough, or commitment-knowledge might still require knowing one's reasons in too many cases to save authority
promise_reason: The reasons/commitments distinction is useful but the claim that confabulation literature doesn't threaten commitment-knowledge needs more defense.

thesis: Accepting the interpretive model commits you to denying that implicit attitudes are genuinely one's own attitudes, because interpretation requires potential rational integration and implicit attitudes are constitutively resistant to such integration.
sketch: Interpretivists ground attitude-attribution in rational integration and coherence-seeking interpretation. But implicit attitudes, by definition, are those that resist rational integration—they persist despite conflicting with explicit commitments and cannot be revised through deliberation. The key premise: if what makes something one's attitude is its availability to interpretive, coherence-seeking processes (as interpretivism requires), then states constitutively resistant to such processes cannot be one's attitudes. This gives interpretivists an unexpected advantage: they can deny that problematic implicit biases are really beliefs/attitudes, avoiding puzzles about how we can simultaneously believe P and not-P. But this commitment is costly—it means interpretivist cannot capture ordinary intuitions that implicit attitudes are ours, just hidden or unconscious.
target: Interpretivists who want to accommodate the full range of attitudes including implicit ones while maintaining that interpretation is constitutive of having attitudes
risk: Interpretivists might accept this consequence gladly, or might show that implicit attitudes do admit of integration given sufficient time/therapy, blocking the 'constitutive resistance' claim
promise_reason: Draws out an interesting commitment of interpretivism about implicit attitudes, though the cost-benefit analysis seems balanced rather than decisive.

thesis: First-person authority exists precisely when interpretation is active rather than complete — we have authority not over what we believe but over what we are in the process of making ourselves believe.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority concerns epistemic access to already-constituted attitudes. But we can distinguish two temporal relations to our own attitudes: archaeological (discovering what we already think) and constructive (settling what we think through the very act of self-ascription). Confabulation studies actually show archaeological self-knowledge failing, but they presuppose subjects have determinate prior attitudes to get wrong. When I sincerely avow 'I intend to quit smoking,' I'm not reporting a pre-existing intention but crystallizing an inchoate one — making it the case that I intend this by committing to it. The authority here is performative, not observational or interpretive. This explains the asymmetry: others can observe my smoking behavior, but they cannot constitute my intention by their ascriptions the way my avowal does. The interpretive theorists are right that we often discover our attitudes through interpretation, but wrong to think all first-person authority works this way.
target: The shared assumption across both camps that first-person authority must concern knowledge of antecedently determinate attitudes, whether through observation (traditional view) or interpretation (Carruthers, Gopnik).
risk: This may only explain authority for future-directed attitudes (intentions, decisions) and fail for backward-looking beliefs about what I've been thinking all along, making it a partial rather than general account.
promise_reason: The archaeological/constructive distinction is clear but the performative account has been explored in the literature already.

thesis: Interpretive self-knowledge and first-person authority come apart because interpretation yields knowledge of attitudes-as-dispositions while authority concerns attitudes-as-commitments, and these are genuinely different states despite sharing the same ordinary language terms.
sketch: When Schwitzgebel shows we're ignorant of our beliefs through interpretation-demanding cases, and when Moran defends first-person authority, they're talking past each other because they're using 'belief' for different things. Interpretation reveals my dispositional profile — what I'm disposed to say, infer, feel in various circumstances. But first-person authority concerns my normative commitments — what I'm willing to stand behind as my view. These can diverge: I might be disposed to reason as though p, yet refuse to commit to p when directly asked. The authority asymmetry holds for commitments (you can't make me have committed to p by your say-so), but not for dispositions (you might know my dispositions better than I do). The confabulation literature threatens only dispositional self-knowledge. The mistake is thinking 'belief' in philosophical debate picks out a single kind of state rather than equivocating between these two.
target: Both sides who assume the empirical literature on confabulation/implicit attitudes and the philosophical literature on first-person authority are studying the same phenomenon under the label 'belief' or 'attitude.'
risk: This looks suspiciously like merely verbal resolution, and critics will ask which of these two 'beliefs' is the real one or whether we're just defining our way to authority over a philosophically uninteresting state.
promise_reason: Diagnosing equivocation between dispositions and commitments is helpful but doesn't clearly advance beyond existing distinction-drawing moves.

thesis: First-person authority survives the interpretive turn because interpretation requires treating the target as rational, but self-interpretation uniquely allows direct intervention on the rationality constraint itself — I can make myself more interpretable by revising toward coherence.
sketch: All interpretation, whether of self or other, requires a rationality assumption (Davidson's principle of charity, Dennett's intentional stance). Others interpret my attitudes by assuming coherence and working backward from behavior; I interpret myself the same way. But here's the asymmetry: when you discover I'm less coherent than expected, you adjust your interpretation. When I discover I'm less coherent than expected, I can adjust my attitudes instead. If I notice my dispositions conflict with what I thought I believed, I don't just reinterpret — I can revise my commitments to restore coherence. This isn't because I have observational access to my attitudes, but because I have agentive control over them. First-person authority isn't about better epistemic access but about constitutive control: my self-ascriptions tend to be correct not because I see my attitudes better, but because I can make my attitudes conform to my ascriptions. The debate has been framed as epistemic (who knows better?) when it's really about agency (who can intervene?).
target: The shared epistemic framing of the debate, where first-person authority is understood as a form of privileged knowledge rather than privileged control.
risk: This explains too much — it makes all self-ascriptions authoritative through rational revision, but we want to distinguish genuine self-knowledge from rationalization or self-deception, which this account may struggle to do.
promise_reason: The intervention/observation contrast is valuable but the agentive control story has been developed by Moran and others.

thesis: Accepting the interpretive view commits you to denying that there are facts about your own fine-grained attitude contents, which means first-person authority trivially survives because there's nothing substantive to be authoritative about.
sketch: The interpretive view holds that attitudes are constituted by patterns in behavior and context, accessible through interpretation. But interpretation, as Quine showed, is radically underdetermined — the same behavioral pattern can be rationalized by indefinitely many attitude attributions. For others, we just pick the simplest interpretation and move on. But the interpretive theorist must say this about self-interpretation too: there's no fact about whether I believe that Hesperus is bright versus believing that Phosphorus is bright, beyond which interpretation best systematizes my dispositions. This means attitude contents are interpretation-relative, not objective features of my mental life. But then the authority question becomes trivial: I'm authoritative about my attitudes in the same deflated sense that I'm authoritative about the meter stick in Paris — it's whatever I say it is, but only because there's no substantial fact to get right or wrong. The interpretive view thus commits you to a kind of attitude anti-realism that makes first-person authority uninteresting rather than false. Interpretive theorists want to naturalize self-knowledge while keeping attitudes robustly real; they can't have both.
target: Interpretive theorists (Carruthers, Gopnik) who assume their view is compatible with attitude realism — that there are determinate facts about what we believe that interpretation is supposed to uncover.
risk: Interpretive theorists might embrace attitude anti-realism and deny this is a problem, or argue that interpretation can be constrained enough to avoid radical underdetermination while remaining genuinely interpretive.
promise_reason: The anti-realist consequence is interesting but whether interpretivists are actually committed to it is contestable.

thesis: Accepting the interpretive account commits one to denying that subjects can have immediate knowledge of attitude content individuation, which collapses the view into an unstable position: if content is partly determined by environmental and social factors that require interpretation to discern, then subjects cannot know what they believe without potentially lengthy empirical investigation of their context.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers argue we know our attitudes through the same interpretive mechanisms we use for others, relying on behavioral and contextual evidence. But attitude content is widely held to be partly individuated by environmental factors (Twin Earth externalism) and social-linguistic practices. If self-knowledge is interpretive, then knowing what I believe requires interpreting not just my behavior but my extended context—causal relations to water vs. XYZ, social role, community linguistic practices. This makes self-knowledge a potentially open-ended empirical project, destroying the phenomenology of immediacy that even interpretivists typically grant. The key premise is that interpretation requires identifying all the relevant content-individuating factors, and if those extend beyond the skin, immediate self-knowledge becomes impossible on interpretivist grounds. Interpretivists thus face a dilemma: either restrict content to narrow/internalist content (abandoning externalism) or accept that we typically don't know what we believe.
target: Gopnik and Carruthers's interpretivist accounts, which aim to preserve some asymmetry and immediacy while adopting the interpretive framework
risk: Interpretivists might bite the bullet and accept that content-knowledge is often incomplete or probabilistic; or distinguish knowing-that-one-believes-something from knowing-exactly-what-one-believes in a way that preserves immediacy for the former
promise_reason: The externalism problem for interpretivism is real but interpretivists have responses about immediate vs. complete knowledge available.

thesis: Moran's agentialist account is unstable: it collapses into either transparent-access epistemic agency (which the empirical literature refutes) or non-epistemic stipulation (which abandons first-person authority as knowledge).
sketch: Moran claims I know my belief that P by answering whether P, exercising rational agency rather than observation. But parse this carefully: either (1) the deliberative procedure reliably tracks what I actually believe, functioning as an epistemic method, or (2) it constitutes/determines what I believe going forward, functioning prescriptively. If (1), we need an explanation of why deliberation is more reliable than behavioral observation for accessing pre-existing attitudes—but the confabulation literature suggests it isn't. We get the reliability of transparent access without its mechanism. If (2), I'm not discovering but deciding, which means I don't have authority about what I believed but only about what I'll believe—this is prospective commitment, not retrospective knowledge. The dilemma's key premise is that knowledge requires a success term (getting it right about something independent of the knowing) while agency requires independence from what's known. Moran needs both simultaneously but can sustain neither horn. First-person authority requires that my self-ascription answers to something, but Moran's agency dissolves the answering-to relation.
target: Moran's agentialist account and its attempt to ground first-person authority in rational agency rather than epistemic access
risk: This might miss that Moran intends a constitutive story all along, where the instability is a feature not a bug—rational self-constitution is its own kind of authority distinct from tracking authority
promise_reason: The dilemma for Moran is clearly stated but agentialists have resources for resisting both horns that aren't engaged here.

thesis: The asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription that grounds first-person authority exists only for attitudes we are currently entertaining, not for standing attitudes, which means the debate has been protecting an asymmetry that applies to a vanishingly small portion of our mental lives.
sketch: All parties assume first-person authority is a general feature of self-knowledge of attitudes. But consider: you ask me whether I believe climate change is anthropogenic. I'm not currently thinking about this, so it's a standing belief. I access it exactly as the interpretivist predicts—by consulting what I've said before, imagining what I'd say now, considering my other commitments. There's no special authority here; I could be wrong in exactly the ways you could be wrong about my beliefs. The asymmetry only exists for attitudes I'm occurrently entertaining right now—and even then, only for those I'm entertaining deliberately rather than passively experiencing. For these narrow cases, Moran-style transparency might work: I know I'm wondering whether P by wondering whether P. But this is a tiny subset. The key premise is that standing attitudes are causally-functionally constituted dispositions that we access through the same kinds of evidence regardless of whose attitudes they are. The debate has been theorizing a marginal case while treating it as paradigmatic, which explains why every theory seems to capture something while missing something else.
target: The shared assumption across all views that first-person authority is a uniform phenomenon applying to attitudes generally
risk: Even standing beliefs might be accessed with asymmetric authority if authority comes from endorsement rather than access—when queried, I don't just report but re-commit, which you cannot do for me
promise_reason: The scope-restriction challenge is important but whether standing attitudes really lack asymmetry is empirically and conceptually contestable.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in privileged epistemic access but in constitutive authority: self-ascriptions of attitudes don't report pre-existing states but rather crystallize indeterminate or inchoate commitments into determinate ones through the very act of avowal.
sketch: The argument turns on distinguishing epistemic from constitutive authority. When I avow 'I believe P,' I'm not merely reporting a belief I independently have—I'm settling what counts as my belief in circumstances where my behavioral dispositions, implicit commitments, and context leave the matter genuinely underdetermined. This explains both the interpretive/constructive element (there's no determinate fact to discover) AND first-person authority (my avowal has special weight because it's performatively constitutive, not because I have better evidence). The key premise: many attitudinal states are metaphysically indeterminate prior to avowal, existing only as clusters of partially inconsistent dispositions. This differs from both discovery models (which assume determinacy) and pure interpretation models (which treat self-ascription as merely evidentially based).
target: The shared assumption across the debate that attitudes are determinate states existing independently of our self-ascriptions, which both privileged-access theorists and interpretivist theorists accept
risk: Seems to make too many of our attitudes metaphysically unstable or indeterminate, potentially collapsing into a form of anti-realism about belief that conflicts with our practices of holding each other responsible for what we believe
promise_reason: Constitutive authority crystallizing indeterminate states is already a standard move in this literature.

thesis: The interpretation we perform on ourselves is not merely like the interpretation we perform on others but is actually constitutive of having determinate attitudinal states at all, making the question of first-person authority ill-formed.
sketch: The debate assumes there are determinate facts about our attitudinal states that we might know well (vindicating first-person authority) or poorly (vindicating the interpretive turn). But if interpretation goes deep enough, there may be no fact of the matter about what I believe independent of my self-interpretive practices. This isn't anti-realism about attitudes generally—your attitudes are determinate relative to the interpretive practices of your linguistic community—but it means my self-interpretation doesn't answer to a prior fact about what I believe; it partially constitutes what I believe. The question 'do I have first-person authority?' then misfires: I have neither privileged epistemic access nor parity with third-person interpreters, because there's nothing fully determinate to have access to until interpretation occurs. The asymmetry between first and third person is real but not epistemic—it's that my interpretation plays a constitutive role that yours doesn't.
target: The shared realist assumption that there are determinate attitude facts prior to and independent of interpretation
risk: This may collapse into implausible anti-realism where I can make myself believe anything just by self-interpreting differently, or fail to explain why some self-interpretations seem clearly mistaken.
promise_reason: The constitutive interpretation view has been explored; claiming the question 'misfires' is provocative but the position itself isn't sufficiently novel.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved on the interpretive model because self-interpretation operates under constitutive constraints that other-interpretation does not: when I settle what I believe, I thereby make it the case, while when you interpret me, you merely discover what is already settled.
sketch: The interpretive theorists assume interpretation is purely epistemic—a matter of discovering what's already there. But self-interpretation is simultaneously constitutive and epistemic. When I deliberate about whether I believe p, the act of settling on an answer doesn't just reveal a pre-existing fact; it completes the determination of that fact. This is why I have authority: not because I have better evidence (I don't), but because my interpretive act has world-to-mind direction of fit while yours has mind-to-world. The key premise is that beliefs are determinables that require the subject's interpretive uptake to become fully determinate, making self-interpretation completion rather than detection.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's parity thesis that self and other-interpretation are symmetric
risk: This may collapse into either Moran's agentialism (if the constitutive role is really about rational commitment) or may fail to explain cases where self-interpretation clearly is discovery (like realizing you've been jealous all along)
promise_reason: The constitutive self-interpretation idea has been developed by others; this version doesn't add enough novelty to the existing literature.

thesis: The agentialist and expressivist accounts presuppose what they claim to explain: they require subjects to already know their commitments or dispositions in order to manifest them through avowals, thus cannot ground first-person authority without circularity.
sketch: Moran says avowal expresses rational commitment; Bar-On says it expresses one's state directly without inference. But both require the subject to already be in a position to express the right state or commitment. How does the subject ensure their avowal expresses belief-that-p rather than hope-that-p or mere supposition? Either they must antecedently identify which state they're in (returning us to the problem), or the avowal is blind expression that coincidentally gets things right (undermining authority). The key premise is that expression requires successful reference to the expressed state, which reintroduces the original epistemic burden. These views trade an epistemic problem for a semantic one that has the same structure.
target: Moran's agentialist account and Bar-On's neo-expressivism
risk: May misunderstand expressivism—perhaps expression doesn't require the subject to pick out the state, but rather constitutes a state of that kind, avoiding the regress
promise_reason: The circularity objection to expressivism is familiar from existing literature; this formulation doesn't add sufficient new pressure.

thesis: First-person authority for belief is an artifact of social deference practices, not a metaphysical or epistemic asymmetry—we grant each other special standing in belief-ascription for pragmatic reasons that have nothing to do with superior access.
sketch: The argument begins by noting that first-person authority manifests primarily in conversational contexts where challenging someone's self-ascription ('You don't really believe that') carries special social costs. The key premise is that this asymmetry can be fully explained by the functional role of belief-talk in coordinating action and holding people accountable: we need a convention that makes people responsible for their avowed beliefs, so we treat sincere first-person reports as default-authoritative regardless of their actual epistemic basis. This explains why the authority is defeasible (we do sometimes override it), context-sensitive (stronger for avowal than for hedged self-interpretation), and extends even to cases where the interpretive account suggests the person is clearly confabulating. The asymmetry isn't that first-person and third-person use different methods, but that we have pragmatic reasons to play different social games with them.
target: Both Moran's agentialist account and Bar-On's neo-expressivism, which take first-person authority to reflect something deep about the nature of self-knowledge or avowal
risk: Cannot explain why first-person authority persists even in non-social contexts (writing in a private journal, forming intentions when alone) or why we ourselves feel the asymmetry internally, not just when dealing with others
promise_reason: Social-pragmatic explanations of authority have been offered before; this version is competent but doesn't advance beyond existing deflationary accounts.

thesis: The interpretive account actually predicts first-person authority for certain attitude types because self-interpretation has systematic evidence advantages: the interpreter has privileged access to memory content, proprioceptive data, and the full phenomenological manifold that accompanies deliberation.
sketch: This argument shows that Carruthers and Gopnik, in emphasizing that we use interpretation for both self and other, overlook that interpretation can yield asymmetric reliability when the evidence base is asymmetric. The key premise is that interpretation is an evidence-sensitive process, and the first-person interpreter has exclusive access to certain categories of evidence (the stream of conscious rehearsal during decision-making, the felt resistance when trying to form certain intentions, the full memory of reasoning history). Just as you can interpret a text better when you have access to draft versions and author's notes, you can interpret your own attitudes better when you have access to the cognitive workspace. This generates first-person authority not as a different kind of knowledge but as an evidential advantage within the same interpretive framework—explaining why it's defeasible (interpretation can still go wrong) but real (the asymmetry in evidence is genuine).
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's symmetric interpretation account, which they present as undermining first-person authority
risk: Schwitzgebel's empirical cases show that even with all this extra evidence, self-interpretation is often unreliable, suggesting the evidence advantage doesn't translate to authority in practice; also doesn't explain the phenomenological sense of direct access rather than inference
promise_reason: The evidential-advantage-within-interpretation move is natural and has been made; it doesn't sufficiently challenge the interpretive framework's commitments.

thesis: Moran's agentialist account collapses into the interpretive view it opposes because deliberative self-knowledge ('What should I believe?') necessarily involves interpreting what one's evidence supports, which is the same interpretive process we use for others.
sketch: Moran argues that we know our beliefs through deliberation—by asking not 'What do I believe about P?' but 'Is P true?'—and this deliberative stance grounds first-person authority. But the argument shows this collapses: when I deliberate about whether P, I must interpret what my evidence supports, assess which considerations are relevant, determine what my experiences mean. This interpretive work is identical in structure to what I do when figuring out what you should believe given your evidence. The key premise is that there's no deliberation without interpretation of reasons, and interpretation of reasons is symmetric between first and third person. The deliberative stance doesn't bypass interpretation; it is a species of interpretation—specifically, interpretation aimed at what to think rather than what one does think. So agentialism cannot ground an authority asymmetry because it reduces to an interpretive process that applies equally to self and other.
target: Moran's agentialist account, which presents deliberation as an alternative to interpretation
risk: Moran might respond that even if deliberation involves interpretation, there's still an asymmetry: only I can settle what I'll believe through deliberation, whereas my interpretation of your evidence only tells me what you should believe, not what you will believe; the constitutive/predictive asymmetry survives
promise_reason: The collapse argument against Moran has been pressed before; this version is clear but doesn't add new dialectical pressure.

thesis: Interpretivism about self-knowledge is unstable because interpretation requires a fixed point of uninterpreted data, but any candidate for that role (behavioral dispositions, phenomenology, neural states) either reinstates privileged access or proves insufficient for generating determinate interpretations.
sketch: Interpretivists claim we know our minds through interpretation of evidence. But interpretation is underdetermination-managing: we select among multiple hypotheses consistent with data. This requires some data that isn't itself an interpretation. For self-interpretation, what could this be? Not raw behavior, because individuating behavior already requires mental concepts (is that motion a wave or a flinch?). Not neural states, because we lack introspective access to those. The interpretivist might say 'phenomenology'—but if we have authoritative access to phenomenology, we have the privileged access that interpretivism denies. Alternatively, if phenomenology is itself interpreted, we face regress. The interpretivist faces a dilemma: either posit some self-presented mental reality (reinstating a non-interpretive ground), or deny any uninterpreted given (making interpretation unconstrained, unable to explain why we converge on stable self-ascriptions). The position collapses either back toward observationalism or forward toward an unworkable holism.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's interpretivist position, which treats self-knowledge as fundamentally similar to other-knowledge
risk: Interpretivists might accept holism and deny the need for uninterpreted foundations; might argue interpretation can be constrained by coherence alone
promise_reason: The regress/fixed-point argument against interpretivism is a standard move in debates about interpretation and holism; competent but familiar.

thesis: The confabulation literature is actually a counterexample to interpretivism rather than observationalism: if we interpreted our attitudes from behavioral evidence as others do, our confabulations would mirror observers' judgments, but systematic divergence shows we access attitudes through a different (if fallible) mechanism.
sketch: Nisbett and Wilson show subjects confabulate reasons, but interpretivists overlook a pattern: our confabulations don't match what third-person interpreters conclude from the same behavioral evidence. When subjects choose the rightmost stockings and confabulate reasons about quality, observers correctly identify position as the cause. If Carruthers were right that we self-interpret from the same evidence observers use, our confabulations should converge with observer judgments (modulo bias). The systematic divergence suggests we access our attitudes through a mechanism unavailable to observers—not infallible introspection, but something like partial access to sub-personal processing that generates confabulations different from purely behavioral interpretation. The key premise: if interpretation from behavioral evidence were symmetric, error patterns would be symmetric; they're not; therefore access is asymmetric.
target: The core interpretive claim that first-person and third-person attitude attribution use the same evidence and methods
risk: The divergence might be explained by interpretive asymmetries like differential access to proprioceptive or phenomenological data (which is still interpretation, just from a richer evidence base) rather than requiring a fundamentally different non-interpretive mechanism
promise_reason: The divergence-of-confabulations argument is clever but the premise that interpretivism predicts convergence is questionable; unlikely to persuade interpretivists.

thesis: The interpretive account and first-person authority are compatible because interpretation from the first-person case has mandatory inputs—phenomenal states and action impulses—that interpretation from the third-person case lacks, giving self-interpretation asymmetric constraint.
sketch: The argument draws a distinction between interpretation-as-inference-structure (which may be symmetric) and interpretation-as-evidential-base (which is asymmetric). Even if I must interpret my beliefs from evidence rather than directly observe them, the evidence available to me differs in kind from what's available to you: I have mandatory access to what it feels like to be me and to incipient action tendencies not yet expressed in behavior. The key premise is that phenomenology and pre-behavioral action readiness are interpretive inputs, not themselves the attitudes being interpreted, but they constrain self-interpretation in ways unavailable to other-interpretation. When I interpret myself as believing p, I'm working from felt dispositions to affirm, phenomenal 'rightness,' and inchoate behavioral preparations. You interpret me from already-executed behavior. This isn't introspective access to beliefs themselves—Schwitzgebel's cases stand—but it's asymmetric constraint on the interpretive process.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's symmetry claim that self-interpretation and other-interpretation work from the same evidence base, which both defenders and critics of their view have generally accepted.
risk: Schwitzgebel might argue these 'mandatory inputs' are themselves subject to massive interpretive uncertainty; unclear whether phenomenal constraint actually helps since phenomenology-attitude links are learned and fallible.
promise_reason: Asymmetric evidential base (phenomenology, action impulses) as constraining interpretation is the standard response to interpretivism; well-worn territory.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved on the interpretive account, but only for intentions and currently occurrent attitudes, not for standing beliefs or dispositions—the latter require interpretation that has no special first-person privilege, generating a principled split in the domain.
sketch: The argument distinguishes between attitudes-as-current-conscious-states and attitudes-as-dispositions. Agentialists like Moran are right about the former: I don't interpret whether I currently intend to φ—my intention-forming is epistemically self-verifying in the right way. But Carruthers is right about standing beliefs: whether I believe that climate change is real (when not currently thinking about it) is a dispositional fact I must interpret from my behavior and reactions, no differently than you would. The key premise is that first-person authority tracks consciousness and agency, not attitude-type. This explains the empirical literature: confabulation studies target standing attitudes and implicit states, not occurrent intentions. It also explains the pull of both views: they're addressing different parts of the mental state space. The split is principled because only currently activated attitudes are subject to agentive self-constitution; dispositional states are theoretical posits for both self and other.
target: Both sides who treat 'attitudes' as a uniform category—either all interpretive or all agentively known—rather than recognizing that different attitude-tokens have different epistemologies.
risk: Unclear how to classify beliefs that are currently occurrent but not intentions; the line between dispositional and occurrent may be too unstable or context-dependent to ground a principled epistemic distinction.
promise_reason: Splitting the domain (authority for occurrent states, not standing beliefs) is a natural compromise position that has been explored.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in epistemic privilege but in constitutive privilege: self-ascriptions of attitudes don't merely report pre-existing states but partially constitute them through a kind of performative uptake.
sketch: The debate assumes attitudes exist independently and the question is how we know them, whether through perception or interpretation. But many attitudes—especially intentions and evaluative beliefs—are essentially response-dependent: they come into determinate existence partly through the subject's endorsement or uptake. When I say 'I intend to φ' I'm not just reporting an intention but crystallizing it from inchoate or competing motivational states. This explains both why interpretation is necessary (the raw materials are underdetermined) and why first-person authority remains (my uptake has constitutive force that yours lacks). The key premise is that the metaphysics of attitudes has been wrongly assumed: they're not detection-independent states but partially constituted by rational self-interpretation.
target: The shared assumption across both observational and interpretive models that attitudes are fully determinate states prior to self-ascription
risk: This may collapse into a form of idealism about mental states that makes pre-reflective attitudes impossible, or may only apply to a narrow class of attitudes (intentions, evaluative beliefs) while leaving the general problem untouched
promise_reason: Constitutive privilege through performative uptake is already well-covered in the expressivist literature.

thesis: The confabulation data doesn't undermine first-person authority but reveals it: we have authority about what we take our reasons to be, and confabulation studies systematically conflate reasons-we-have with reasons-we-take-ourselves-to-have.
sketch: Nisbett and Wilson show subjects misreport the causes of their choices (e.g., choosing right-side items while citing quality). But this is a counterexample to first-person authority only if we assume authority extends to causal-explanatory reasons. If instead authority concerns normative reasons—the considerations that figure in our rational deliberation—the studies are perfectly compatible with authority. When subjects say 'I chose this for its quality,' they correctly report what they took to be their reason, even if they're wrong about what caused their choice. The key premise is that a properly Moorean account of first-person authority concerns the space of reasons, not the space of causes, and confabulation studies systematically fail to distinguish these.
target: The widespread assumption that confabulation studies directly undermine first-person authority rather than revealing conceptual confusion about what authority covers
risk: This may seem to trivialize first-person authority by restricting it to a normatively-loaded domain, or may face cases where subjects confabulate even about what they took their reasons to be during deliberation
promise_reason: The normative/causal reasons distinction has been deployed before to handle confabulation; this is a competent restatement rather than novel.

thesis: Confabulation studies show not that we lack introspective access but that we have systematic access to our standing commitment-to-justify rather than to causal-historical origins.
sketch: Nisbett-Wilson cases are standardly read as showing we confabulate about our mental states. But draw a distinction between two aspects of attitudes: their causal-historical provenance (what actually caused them) and their rational-normative position (what considerations currently support them and what we're committed to defending them with). Confabulation occurs when subjects accurately report the latter but err about the former. We have genuine introspective access to our justificatory commitments—what we're prepared to defend—even when we lack access to genesis. This preserves first-person authority about the normative dimension of attitudes while accepting interpretivist insights about our blindness to causes. The key premise: attitudes are individuated partly by normative relations, not just causes.
target: The shared assumption in the confabulation literature that if we're wrong about etiology, we lack access to the attitude itself
risk: May be forced to say that the 'real' attitude is whichever one wins out between causal origin and current justificatory commitment, recreating the access problem at a higher level
promise_reason: Similar to thesis 4 but weaker—the justificatory commitment vs. causal origin distinction is familiar territory in this literature.

thesis: The apparent asymmetry between self and other-ascription is an artifact of differential social consequences, not differential epistemic access: we treat avowals as authoritative because challenging them is socially costly in a way that challenging other-ascriptions is not.
sketch: First-person authority appears to be an epistemic asymmetry requiring special explanation. But reframe it as a social-practical asymmetry: when you sincerely avow 'I believe P,' challenging you carries higher social costs (implying bad faith, fracturing interaction, triggering defensiveness) than challenging 'She believes P' does. We *treat* avowals as authoritative not because speakers have better evidence, but because the social practice of accepting sincere avowals is more stable than the alternative. This explains why authority is defeasible (we override it when stakes are high enough) and why it doesn't extend to all self-attributions (not to unconscious states where the social norm doesn't apply). The key premise: an observed regularity in accepting first-person claims doesn't entail an epistemic difference; it could be sustained by differential costs of challenge.
target: Both sides of the debate who treat the authority asymmetry as a primarily epistemic phenomenon requiring epistemic explanation
risk: Cannot explain why the social practice arose in the first place—why treating avowals as authoritative became the stable norm unless there was some underlying epistemic asymmetry to track
promise_reason: Social-pragmatic debunking has been attempted before; this version doesn't add enough to change the conversation.

thesis: The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically misidentify which attitudes we are introspecting—we have genuine access to our motivating attitudes but confabulate when asked about our justifying reasons, mistaking the former for the latter.
sketch: Standard interpretations of Nisbett and Wilson take subjects to be wholly confabulating—making up attitudes they don't have. But reanalyze the classic experiments: when subjects choose stockings from a display and cite quality rather than position, they aren't confabulating a preference (they genuinely preferred that stocking) but confabulating a reason-explanation for the preference. The mistake is metarepresentational: they have introspective access to what moved them (an attraction to rightward items) but misrepresent this motivation as a rational justification (quality assessment). This dissolves the apparent conflict: introspection delivers attitudes reliably, but our self-understanding of which attitude-type we're accessing is theory-laden and corruptible. The debate falsely assumes that if introspection fails for reason-explanation, it fails entirely. The key premise is that accessing an attitude and correctly categorizing what kind of attitude it is are separable achievements.
target: Both sides' shared assumption that confabulation data threatens introspective access as such
risk: This might merely relocate the problem—if we can't introspect which kind of attitude we're introspecting, the asymmetry with other-knowledge collapses at a different level
promise_reason: Another variant of distinguishing attitude-types to save introspection from confabulation data; the metarepresentational twist is minor.

thesis: Holding that implicit attitudes are genuine attitudes commits you to denying first-person authority even for explicit attitudes, because the interpretation required to identify implicit attitudes as attitudes undermines the boundary between interpreted and non-interpreted mental states.
sketch: Many philosophers accept both that implicit biases are genuine attitudes (beliefs or preferences) and that we need special interpretation to identify them—they're not introspectively available. But if attitudes can be fully genuine while requiring interpretation for identification, what makes explicit 'introspectively available' attitudes non-interpreted? The natural answer is that explicit attitudes are constituted by introspective seemings. But this recreates the pre-interpretive access model that the implicit attitudes literature was supposed to undermine. Alternatively, explicit attitudes are also interpreted, just more easily—but then the distinction between first-person and third-person attribution collapses entirely, as both are equally interpretive. The dialectic forces a choice: either implicit 'attitudes' aren't really attitudes (they're mere dispositions we interpret as if they were attitudes), or explicit attitudes have no special first-person status. You cannot consistently maintain both that implicit attitudes are real attitudes and that explicit attitudes enjoy first-person authority. The key premise is that attitude-hood cannot come in epistemically different varieties without collapsing into a distinction between real attitudes and interpreted-as-if attitudes.
target: Theorists like Schwitzgebel who accept implicit attitudes as genuine while trying to preserve some first-person authority for explicit attitudes
risk: There might be a principled way to distinguish attitude-types by their functional role that makes different epistemic access appropriate for different types without this being ad hoc
promise_reason: The tension between implicit and explicit attitudes under interpretivism has been extensively discussed.

thesis: The agentialist and neo-expressivist accounts are unstable because they require that self-ascriptions are answerable to deliberative and expressive norms respectively, but meeting those norms requires already knowing what one's attitudes are, creating explanatory circularity.
sketch: Moran claims authority derives from the transparency condition—answering 'Do I believe p?' by answering 'Is p true?' But deploying this method requires already knowing whether the question is asking about belief specifically versus some other attitude (hope, supposition, etc.), which requires prior attitude identification. Similarly, Bar-On's account says avowals express attitudes rather than report them, grounding authority in expressive correctness. But expressing belief-that-p (versus fearing-that-p or imagining-that-p) correctly requires already distinguishing which attitude you're expressing, which reintroduces the identification problem these accounts meant to bypass. Both accounts try to ground self-knowledge in something other than state-identification (deliberation or expression), but that grounding relation itself presupposes successful attitude identification. They don't eliminate the need for interpretive or introspective identification; they just postpone addressing it. The accounts thus collapse back into either observationalism (we must somehow identify attitudes pre-deliberatively) or interpretivism (we identify them through the same evidence everyone else uses).
target: Moran's agentialist account and Bar-On's neo-expressivism, showing they don't actually offer a third alternative
risk: These theorists might argue the circularity is benign or that pre-reflective practical knowledge suffices for norm-guidance without requiring explicit attitude identification
promise_reason: The circularity objection to Moran and Bar-On has been raised before; this formulation is clear but doesn't add substantial new pressure.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in epistemic but in constitutive priority: self-ascriptions of belief constitute refinements or disambiguations of indeterminate prior states rather than reports of determinate pre-existing ones.
sketch: The debate assumes determinate attitudinal states that we either perceive or interpret, but Schwitzgebel's cases suggest massive indeterminacy in our beliefs. The argument turns on recognizing that avowed self-ascriptions don't merely report but actually settle what we believe in borderline cases—they are acts of self-constitution rather than self-discovery. This explains first-person authority without requiring privileged epistemic access: I have authority not because I'm better positioned to discover what I already believe, but because my sincere avowal settles what was previously unsettled. The interpretive evidence constrains but underdetermines; avowal completes. This dissolves the tension because interpretation and authority operate at different stages: interpretation reveals the space of eligible attitudes, avowal selects among them.
target: The shared assumption among both observationalists and interpretivists that there are fully determinate attitudinal states to be known
risk: Cannot explain cases where we seem straightforwardly wrong about our beliefs, or where first-person authority seems to apply to past beliefs that can no longer be constituted by present avowal
promise_reason: Self-ascription settling indeterminate states is a standard move in contemporary debates.

thesis: Accepting the interpretive model commits you to rejecting first-person/third-person asymmetry for occurrent thoughts and experiences, not just for standing attitudes—a commitment interpretivists have failed to recognize and which reveals the view's instability.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers restrict their account to standing attitudes (beliefs, desires) while tacitly assuming direct access to occurrent thoughts and experiences which provide the interpretive base. But the same confabulation evidence extends to occurrent states: we misidentify what we're currently experiencing (pain/pressure confusion), what we're currently thinking (verbal thoughts we attribute to ourselves but couldn't accurately report), and what we're currently feeling (misattributed arousal). The key premise: there is no principled distinction between standing and occurrent states that would allow interpretation for one but not the other—both are attitude-types requiring content-ascription, both show the same confabulation patterns. Thus the interpretive view must go global, interpreting even occurrent experience. But this collapses into either eliminativism (there are no occurrent states as traditionally conceived) or requires a new interpretive base, forcing infinite regress. Interpretivists cannot help themselves to a privileged foundation without abandoning what motivated their view.
target: Carruthers and other interpretivists who implicitly exempt occurrent states from interpretation
risk: Interpretivists might accept the commitment and defend global interpretation, or might find a principled distinction between standing and occurrent states
promise_reason: The extension to occurrent states has been discussed; interpretivists like Schwitzgebel already embrace this commitment rather than seeing it as a reductio.

thesis: First-person authority survives the interpretive turn not despite interpretation but because self-interpretation uniquely involves the interpreter's capacity to make true what they interpret themselves as believing.
sketch: The debate assumes interpretation is purely epistemic—a matter of getting the facts right about pre-existing states. But self-interpretation is constitutive in a way other-interpretation cannot be: when I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation can settle an otherwise indeterminate matter, creating the very belief it purports to discover. The key premise is that many of our attitudes exist in a superposed or inchoate state until interpretation crystallizes them. This isn't just expressivist performance (as in Bar-On) but genuine retroactive determination. I have authority not because I observe better or express directly, but because my interpretive verdict has world-to-mind direction of fit regarding my own mind. This explains why therapeutic contexts work: the patient's accepted interpretation doesn't just reveal but constitutes their psychological reality.
target: The shared assumption across Carruthers, Gopnik, Moran, and Bar-On that mental states are determinate facts awaiting discovery through either observation or expression
risk: Collapses into voluntarism about belief or fails to distinguish genuine self-knowledge from self-deception; may not explain authority about occurrent phenomenal states where determinacy seems non-negotiable
promise_reason: The self-fulfilling interpretation idea appears in various forms in the existing literature; this version doesn't add enough to stand out.

thesis: Interpretivism explains away rather than explains first-person authority: when we interpret ourselves off behavioral evidence, what we gain isn't self-knowledge but merely self-attribution, and the residual appearance of authority is just reluctance to second-guess oneself on pragmatic grounds.
sketch: This challenges the conciliatory move many make—that interpretivism can preserve authority on different grounds. The key premise: genuine knowledge requires the possibility of discovery, but if I'm interpreting myself off the same evidence available to others, then there's nothing to discover beyond what others could discover. The cases treated as first-person authority are actually just cases where social practice defers to the self-interpreter (pragmatic deference). Counterexample: consider someone recovering from manipulation or emerging from self-deception—the therapist often has superior knowledge of the patient's beliefs/desires than the patient does. If interpretivism is right, this should be normal rather than pathological, since the therapist has better interpretive skills plus the same behavioral data. That we find such cases pathological shows we're not interpretivists about self-knowledge. The diagnosis: philosophers mistake pragmatic deference (it's socially useful to let people be authority about their attitudes) for epistemic privilege. First-person authority doesn't survive the interpretive turn because there was nothing there to survive—just a useful social convention.
target: The reconciliation project itself; the shared assumption that first-person authority is a robust explanandum rather than an artifact of folk practice that should be explained away
risk: Too revisionary—seems to deny phenomenologically obvious asymmetries in access; may conflate unusual pathological cases with the ordinary case; vulnerable to the objection that even pragmatic deference requires some ground, and that ground is what needs explaining
promise_reason: The deflationary move (authority is just pragmatic deference) has been made; this version doesn't add sufficient new pressure to the conciliatory interpretivist positions.

thesis: First-person authority is an artifact of conversational norms that prohibit challenging sincere avowals, not an epistemic asymmetry; what needs explaining is why we've evolved these norms, not how self-knowledge works.
sketch: The asymmetry between 'You believe P' (challengeable) and 'I believe P' (authoritative) isn't epistemic but social-pragmatic. Evolutionary game theory shows that allowing challenges to sincere self-ascriptions creates coordination problems—if I can't reliably communicate my commitments, cooperative planning breaks down. The norm of first-person authority is a solution: we treat sincere avowals as conversationally unchallengeable not because speakers have special access, but because challenge-immune self-ascription enables commitment-making. This explains why authority persists even given confabulation: the social function doesn't require accuracy, only reliable commitment. Moran and Bar-On mistake a pragmatic prohibition on challenge for an epistemic entitlement to defer to the speaker. The 'problem' of reconciling interpretivism with authority dissolves—they operate at different levels. We interpret each other constantly, including ourselves, but maintain a social fiction of first-person authority because it's coordination-enabling. The philosophical puzzle arises from reifying this useful fiction into a metaphysical fact about access.
target: Everyone in the debate who treats first-person authority as a datum about knowledge rather than a pragmatic-normative construct
risk: Doesn't explain why we feel authoritative about our attitudes even in non-social contexts (private reflection), and may be empirically undermined if similar coordination could be achieved through other means.
promise_reason: Pure social-pragmatic deflationism has been explored; treating authority as merely conventional faces well-known objections this sketch doesn't address.

thesis: First-person authority about our attitudes is grounded not in privileged access to what we believe but in constitutive authority over what counts as believing it—the difference between self-interpretation and other-interpretation is that only self-interpretation can make itself true by fiat.
sketch: The debate assumes that both self- and other-interpretation aim at the same target (what I already believe) and differ only epistemologically. But distinguish discovery-interpretation from constitutive-interpretation: when I sincerely avow 'I believe P,' I'm not just reporting but partly determining the attitude's rational standing in my mental economy. The key premise is that beliefs are individuated not just by causal/functional role but by rational integration, and only the subject has authority to ratify an interpretation as rationally binding. This explains why I can be wrong about causal origins (Nisbett & Wilson) but authoritative about rational commitments—I'm doing different things.
target: Both Carruthers/Gopnik (who treat all self-interpretation as discovery) and Moran (who grounds authority in agentive reasons-responsiveness without explaining why that yields epistemic authority)
