risk: Collapses into constitutivism about all mental states, making sincere error about our beliefs impossible and turning psychology into a branch of decision theory
promise_reason: Constitutive authority making interpretation true by fiat is well-trodden ground.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in epistemic privilege but in constitutive control: self-ascriptions of attitudes are authoritative because making them can rationally commit you to aligning the attitude with the ascription, whereas ascribing attitudes to others creates no such commitment.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be explained epistemically (privileged access vs. interpretation). But consider that saying 'I intend to φ' can itself generate rational pressure to φ in a way that saying 'She intends to φ' cannot affect her intentions. The authority isn't about knowing better what's already there, but about a distinctive normative relationship: self-ascriptions can be simultaneously descriptive and commitment-generating. This explains both why interpretation is necessary (there's no pre-interpretive fact of the matter to observe) and why self-ascription differs from other-ascription (only the former creates rational pressure for attitude-ascription alignment). The key premise is that rational agents treat their own sincere avowals as generating normative constraints on subsequent attitude formation.
target: The shared assumption across Carruthers, Gopnik, Moran, and Bar-On that first-person authority must be explained by a distinctive way of knowing pre-existing attitudes
risk: Cannot explain cases of self-knowledge about attitudes we're confident we won't revise (e.g., 'I believe Paris is in France'), where constitutive control seems irrelevant
promise_reason: The constitutive-control move is already prominent in the literature (Moran, Bilgrami); this restates rather than advances it.

thesis: The interpretive view and first-person authority are compatible because interpretation operates under different rational constraints in the first-person case: we interpret ourselves under a presumption of intelligibility that we can violate for others, making self-interpretation inherently more constrained and thus more reliable.
sketch: Interpreters of others can attribute irrationality, inconsistency, or unintelligibility when evidence runs out. But Davidson's principle of charity shows that self-interpretation cannot coherently proceed this way: treating oneself as fundamentally irrational or unintelligible defeats the conditions for having a perspective from which to interpret at all. This means first-person interpretation operates under a constitutive rational constraint: we must interpret ourselves as making sense. This constraint doesn't give us infallible access, but it does make self-interpretation systematically more constrained than other-interpretation, because we cannot invoke 'they're just being irrational' as an interpretive resource. Therefore, accepting the interpretive view commits you to accepting an asymmetry that grounds a deflationary version of first-person authority.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's claim that self-interpretation and other-interpretation are fundamentally symmetric processes
risk: The constraint might be too weak to explain the phenomenology of immediate self-knowledge, or it might collapse into a version of rationalism about self-knowledge
promise_reason: The charity-constraint point about self-interpretation is Davidsonian orthodoxy; applying it here is competent but the argument has been made.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved under interpretation because attitudes aren't fully determinate until self-ascription: the interpretive process doesn't discover but partially constitutes the attitude, giving self-interpretation a kind of priority-by-completion that other-interpretation lacks.
sketch: The debate assumes attitudes exist determinately pre-interpretation, with the only question being how we know them. But consider cases of ambiguous evidence where you genuinely don't know whether you believe P until you commit to a self-ascription. The interpretive act doesn't just report but completes an indeterminate state. This isn't just confabulation creating a false belief about a determinate fact—it's determination of an indeterminate fact. This provides a counterexample to the shared premise that interpretation is purely epistemic (discovering what's there). If attitudes can be indeterminate until self-ascription, then self-interpretation has a constitutive role others' interpretations lack: only you can complete your own indeterminate attitudes by committing to an interpretation. This grounds first-person authority without denying that interpretation is doing work.
target: The shared assumption between interpretivists and their critics that attitudes are determinate states that exist independently of our attempts to know them
risk: Risks being ad hoc unless there's independent reason to think attitudes are indeterminate; might also struggle with cases where we seem to discover surprising determinate facts about ourselves
promise_reason: Priority-by-completion of indeterminate attitudes is already a recognized position.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in privileged access to attitudes themselves but in privileged authority over what interpretation-settling performances count as sincere.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be explained by some epistemic asymmetry regarding mental states themselves. But there's a neglected distinction between knowing what you believe and having authority over which verbal/behavioral performances get to count as genuine expressions rather than strategic moves. Even if self-interpretation is as fallible as other-interpretation regarding what attitudes you antecedently have, you retain constitutive authority over which interpretive performances are made in good faith versus manipulatively. The agentialist can grant full interpretivism about discovering attitudes while preserving authority over the speech acts that make new attitudes explicit. This explains why 'I believe P' can be simultaneously a discovery (interpretive) and yet authoritative in a way third-person ascriptions aren't.
target: The shared assumption that first-person authority requires privileged epistemic access to pre-existing attitudes
risk: This may collapse into a merely pragmatic or conversational authority rather than capturing the metaphysical asymmetry that motivates agentialist and expressivist accounts
promise_reason: Authority over sincerity rather than content is an interesting move but too narrow—it doesn't explain authority about what one believes, only about speech-act status.

thesis: First-person authority survives interpretivism because our own interpretive activity creates an evidential trace unavailable to external interpreters: the phenomenology of interpretive effort itself.
sketch: Accept interpretivism: you discover your attitudes by interpreting evidence. But notice that interpreters themselves have cognitive phenomenology—the experience of considering, weighing, finding considerations salient. When you interpret yourself, this phenomenology becomes part of your evidence base in a way it can't for external interpreters. Not because it's infallible access to attitudes, but because the very act of self-interpretation generates phenomenal evidence about what you find compelling, what feels strained, what comes naturally. Schwitzgebel's confabulation cases actually reveal this: subjects aren't randomly wrong but systematically biased by what interpretations feel right. This interpretive phenomenology grounds a residual first-person authority even on full interpretivism. External interpreters lack access not to your attitudes but to your experience of interpreting yourself.
target: Pure interpretivist accounts that eliminate all first-person/third-person asymmetry
risk: This reintroduces a problematic inner perception model through the back door, or the phenomenology of interpretation might itself require interpretation and start a regress
promise_reason: Interpretive phenomenology as evidence has been discussed (Pitt, Smithies on cognitive phenomenology); this applies it competently but doesn't break new ground.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in privileged access to mental states but in the social practice of holding subjects responsible for coherence between avowal and subsequent action.
sketch: The argument begins by noting that when someone sincerely avows a belief or intention, we treat them as committed to acting consistently with it—not because they have special epistemic access, but because avowal creates a normative bind. The asymmetry between self- and other-ascription emerges not from different epistemic routes but from different normative positions: only the subject can bind themselves through avowal. This explains why we defer to self-ascriptions while still explaining confabulation cases—the authority attaches to the speech act of avowal itself, not to any prior cognitive state the avowal reports. The key premise is that first-person authority is constituted by, rather than explained by, the practice of treating avowals as commitment-creating.
target: Both expressivist accounts (Bar-On) that treat avowals as groundless expressions and interpretivist accounts (Carruthers) that treat them as evidence-based interpretations
risk: Cannot adequately distinguish genuine self-knowledge from mere self-binding rhetoric, and may collapse into a purely external, third-personal account that abandons the phenomenology of introspection entirely
promise_reason: The social-practice grounding for authority has been developed by expressivist and neo-Wittgensteinian approaches; this restates that position clearly but not originally.

thesis: The interpretive turn and first-person authority are compatible because interpretation of one's own attitudes is subject to constitutive rational constraints that interpretation of others' attitudes escapes.
sketch: When I interpret my own belief that P, I cannot coherently maintain that interpretation while simultaneously judging P to be false—this is Moore's paradox territory. But when I interpret your belief that P, I face no such constraint. This reveals that self-interpretation operates under constitutive rational norms (transparency conditions) that make it simultaneously interpretive and authoritative. The key distinction is between interpretation that is constitutively constrained by rational norms internal to the attitude being interpreted versus interpretation that faces only evidential constraints. Moran's deliberative transparency falls out as a special case: when I ask whether I believe P, I answer by asking whether P, because self-interpretation is rationally required to respect this connection in a way other-interpretation is not.
target: Interpretivist accounts (Carruthers, Gopnik) that assume self-interpretation and other-interpretation differ only in available evidence, not in rational structure
risk: The constitutive constraints may turn out to be merely normative ideals we violate in confabulation cases, rather than structural features that explain authority even in non-ideal cases
promise_reason: The transparency-constraint point closely parallels thesis 3 and existing Moran-inspired arguments; it's competent but covers familiar ground.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in epistemic privilege but in constitutive privilege: self-ascriptions of belief partly constitute what one believes in a way that other-ascriptions cannot.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be either epistemic (better access) or illusory. But there's a third option: Avowing 'I believe P' in contexts where one is interpretively self-opaque doesn't report a pre-existing state but partially fixes what one believes, completing an otherwise indeterminate psychological profile. The interpretive evidence underdetermines belief attribution even from the first-person perspective, but the subject's self-ascription breaks the tie constitutively rather than epistemically. This explains why first-person authority survives interpretive opacity: it's not that I see my belief better than you do, but that my saying 'I believe P' makes it more the case that I believe P than your saying 'You believe P' does. The key premise: mental states admit of indeterminacy that authoritative self-ascription can resolve.
target: Both epistemicists about first-person authority (like traditional introspectionists) and skeptics (like Carruthers) who assume authority must be evidential
risk: May collapse into a form of voluntarism about belief that's independently implausible, or fail to explain cases where self-ascription is clearly just wrong
promise_reason: Constitutive privilege is the standard move; this formulation doesn't advance it.

thesis: The asymmetry between self and other-ascription exists only for beliefs about one's own mental states, not for any other beliefs, revealing that 'first-person authority' is actually just the trivial authority that comes from being the thing described.
sketch: Consider: I have 'first-person authority' about whether my shirt is wet in the sense that if I'm actually wearing the shirt, I can feel wetness directly while you must observe from outside. This isn't a deep epistemic asymmetry about belief-formation—it's just that I'm the one in contact with the shirt. Similarly, when it comes to beliefs, I have authority about 'my current believing' not because of privileged introspective access but because I am the process of believing, and being a process gives you information about that process that outside observation lacks—not through inner perception but through immediate involvement. The debate wrongly treats this as mysterious epistemic authority requiring special explanation. On this view, the confabulation literature shows we lack privileged access to mental states as objects, but we retain the non-mysterious 'authority' of being the process itself, which doesn't require interpretation or observation.
target: Both introspectionists and interpretivists who treat first-person authority as requiring philosophical explanation beyond the trivial sense of 'being the thing in question'
risk: The analogy to physical properties may break down—being a belief-process doesn't clearly give information about it the way being in contact with wetness does; this might just relabel rather than explain the phenomenon
promise_reason: The 'being the process' idea is intriguing but too underdeveloped to clearly distinguish from existing positions on non-observational knowledge.

thesis: The interpretive view collapses into a hybrid position once we recognize that interpretation itself requires privileged access to the phenomenology of salience—what features of behavior or context strike one as significant is only accessible first-personally.
sketch: Carruthers and Gopnik argue we interpret ourselves from behavioral/contextual evidence using the same theory we apply to others. But interpretation isn't mechanical—it requires noticing certain patterns and not others, finding some features salient and others ignorable. Which aspects of my behavior strike me as relevant when I interpret my belief about p? I have direct access to this phenomenology of salience in my own case that I lack for others—I feel which considerations grab me, which seem off, which resonate. This selective attention is itself an attitudinal state that guides interpretation but cannot itself be interpreted without vicious regress (what makes the meta-interpretation of my salience patterns salient?). So pure interpretivism is unstable: to get interpretation started, we need non-interpretive access to at least our interpretive orientations. The view necessarily collapses into: interpretation built on a foundation of privileged access to one's own cognitive phenomenology.
target: Pure interpretivism as defended by Carruthers and Gopnik
risk: The phenomenology of salience might itself be interpreted from lower-level patterns (evolutionary or neural), blocking the regress without requiring privileged access
promise_reason: The phenomenology-of-salience point has been made in debates about cognitive phenomenology; application here is competent but not novel.

thesis: First-person authority is grounded not in privileged access to states but in the constitutive priority of avowal: the act of self-ascribing a belief is metaphysically prior to the existence of any settled fact about whether one has that belief.
sketch: The debate assumes there's a determinate fact about what I believe that I then either observe or interpret. But confabulation studies and implicit bias research show massive instability in what we 'find' when we introspect. The key premise: this instability isn't epistemic failure but reveals that for many attitudes, there is no settled fact until avowal creates one. Self-ascription doesn't report a prior state—it partially constitutes it by taking an agential stance that fixes an otherwise indeterminate manifold of dispositions. This explains asymmetry without requiring privileged access: you can't constitute my beliefs, but I can constitute my own. The authority isn't epistemic but metaphysical-generative.
target: The shared assumption across both observationalists and interpretivists that attitudes are determinate states that exist prior to and independent of self-ascription
risk: Cannot handle clear cases of false self-ascription (I sincerely avow believing p while obviously not believing p) without collapsing into revisionism that makes systematic self-deception impossible
promise_reason: Very similar to theses 0 and 5; the metaphysical-priority framing doesn't add enough to warrant separate treatment.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved not despite interpretation but because self-interpretation operates under a constitutive constraint that other-interpretation lacks: the requirement of agential coherence with one's ongoing practical commitments.
sketch: The interpretive turn wrongly assumes interpretation works the same way in both first- and third-person cases. But self-interpretation is not merely evidence-gathering; it operates under a distinctive rational constraint: my interpretation must be one I can incorporate into my ongoing practical identity without rational fragmentation. When I interpret my own belief, I'm simultaneously positioning myself to act on that interpretation going forward. This creates a rational pressure toward coherence that doesn't apply when interpreting others—I can attribute inconsistent beliefs to you without practical cost, but self-attributing them requires me to either resolve the conflict or accept akrasia. This constraint doesn't give me infallible access, but it does explain why self-ascriptions carry a distinctive authority: they're constrained by requirements of practical coherence that other-ascriptions escape. The key premise is that self-interpretation is simultaneously world-describing and will-forming in a way other-interpretation is not.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's symmetrical interpretation thesis, which treats self- and other-interpretation as differing only in evidence available
risk: The distinction might collapse if we can show that interpretations of others also face rational coherence constraints when those others are people we're deeply entangled with (close friends, collaborators), suggesting the asymmetry is merely one of degree.
promise_reason: Essentially repeats thesis 14's practical-coherence constraint without adding sufficient new content to justify separate consideration.

thesis: The interpretivist position is unstable because interpretation requires a stable base of non-interpreted mental states to interpret from, but interpretivism cannot specify which states serve this role without either circularity or arbitrariness.
sketch: Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our attitudes by interpreting behavioral and contextual evidence using the same theory-of-mind machinery we use for others. But interpretation is inference from evidence to conclusion—if I infer my belief that P from my behavior, I must already know what my behavior is and what it indicates. This requires non-interpreted knowledge of some mental states (at minimum, my perceptual states and my inferential dispositions). The key premise: interpretivists cannot say which states are known non-interpretively without either arbitrarily privileging some states, or saying 'all the way down' is interpretation (which is circular—interpretation presupposes non-interpreted inputs). When pressed, interpretivists retreat to phenomenal states as the non-interpreted base, but this concedes that we have non-interpretive self-knowledge of mental states, which was supposed to be what confabulation studies ruled out.
target: Strong interpretivist positions like Carruthers and Gopnik that model self-knowledge primarily on other-knowledge via theory-of-mind
risk: Interpretivists may bite the bullet and accept that phenomenal states are known non-interpretively while maintaining that propositional attitudes specifically require interpretation, or argue for coherentist rather than foundationalist interpretation where no states serve as a fixed base
promise_reason: The 'base states' objection to interpretivism is familiar from foundationalist epistemology debates; interpretivists have standard responses.

thesis: First-person authority survives the interpretive turn not because self-interpretation has privileged access to evidence, but because the self-interpreter has unique authority to terminate the interpretive process—a volitional rather than epistemic asymmetry.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be grounded in epistemic advantage (either observational or agential). But there's a conflated distinction between authority-as-reliability and authority-as-finality. When I avow a belief, my special authority isn't that I'm more likely to be right, but that challenges to my self-ascription face a different pragmatic barrier: while you can always demand I provide more evidence for attributing belief B to myself, I can—by the very act of sincere avowal—make it the case that further interpretation is beside the point. This is why Moore-paradoxical statements ('I believe P but P is false') are defective in first-person but not third-person: the first-person avowal carries a commitment-constituting force that closes interpretive space. The asymmetry is in our differing relationships to the speech act, not to the evidence.
target: Both Moran's agentialism and the pure interpretivist camp (Carruthers, Gopnik), who both assume authority requires epistemic justification
risk: This might collapse into a performative or expressivist account that Bar-On already defends, just redescribed; or it may not actually preserve what we mean by 'authority' if that authority is compatible with systematic error
promise_reason: Authority-as-finality versus authority-as-reliability has been discussed; the speech-act angle adds little that's new to existing pragmatic accounts.

thesis: Implicit attitudes reveal that first-person authority is domain-restricted to attitudes we can make explicit through reasoning, and this restriction shows the agentialist account is correct but self-limiting: authority extends only as far as rational agency does.
sketch: The implicit attitudes literature is usually treated as a problem for all accounts of first-person authority. But it actually vindicates a restricted version of Moran's agentialism while showing why that view must accept sharp limits. Moran grounds first-person authority in our stance as rational agents who settle what to believe by reasoning about the world. But implicit attitudes are precisely those attitudes that are insulated from this rational-agential process—they don't respond to my deliberating about reasons. The key move: accepting Moran's account commits you to denying first-person authority for implicit attitudes, since they lie outside the rational-agential domain. This isn't a bug but reveals the underlying structure: we have authority where we have rational control, and confabulation occurs exactly where we attempt to assert authority beyond that domain. This explains both why we're authoritative about explicit beliefs and why we confabulate about implicit ones—it's the same mechanism.
target: Moran's agentialism, which needs to either accept this limitation or explain why rational agency extends to implicit attitudes despite their recalcitrance to reasoning
risk: The line between explicit and implicit attitudes may be too vague or fluid to support a principled distinction about authority; or Moran might already accept this limitation, making it not a new commitment but an existing feature
promise_reason: This is essentially conceding Moran's limits rather than defending him; the restriction strategy has been explored and doesn't advance the debate much.

thesis: The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically misidentify which mental states are attitudinal states versus which are merely enabling conditions.
sketch: Nisbett-Wilson cases involve subjects correctly detecting genuine mental states (the preference, the attraction) but misattributing their etiology—they mistake an enabling causal condition (the music, the position) for a reason-giving attitude. The key premise is that attitudes are constituted by inferential role, not mere causal efficacy: the music enabled the preference but wasn't what the preference was about. When subjects confabulate, they accurately introspect the preference itself (showing introspection works) but err in reconstructing its rational-causal history (a different cognitive task). This distinction reclassifies the debate: confabulation threatens our grasp of attitude genealogy, not attitude presence. We can preserve both observational introspection for current attitudes and the interpretive story for understanding their sources. First-person authority holds for 'what I believe/intend' but not for 'why I believe/intend it.'
target: Schwitzgebel and Carruthers, who take confabulation evidence to undermine introspective access to attitudes themselves
risk: Subjects in confabulation studies often seem genuinely uncertain about the preference itself, not just its causes, suggesting the attitude wasn't determinately there to introspect
promise_reason: Distinguishing attitude-presence from attitude-genealogy is useful but doesn't fundamentally challenge either main position; too accommodating.

thesis: Interpretivism about self-knowledge is unstable because the interpreter must already possess non-interpreted attitudes (at minimum: the intention to self-interpret) that cannot themselves be known interpretively on pain of regress.
sketch: Carruthers-style interpretivism claims we know our attitudes by interpreting evidence. But interpretation is itself an intentional activity requiring attitudes: the intention to interpret, beliefs about which interpretive principles to apply, preferences among competing interpretations. If these interpretive-enabling attitudes are also known only through interpretation, we face regress. The interpretivist must grant that at least some attitudes (those constituting the interpretive activity itself) are known non-interpretively—through direct awareness, stipulation, or constitution. But once we admit any attitudes are knowable non-interpretively, the principled motivation for interpretivism elsewhere collapses: if direct access works for interpretive intentions, why not for other attitudes? The position thus collapses into either regress or a hybrid view where interpretation rests on a foundation of non-interpreted self-knowledge, undermining the interpretive turn's claim to comprehensiveness.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's comprehensive interpretivism about self-knowledge
risk: Interpretivists might accept a narrow foundation of non-interpreted states (current intentions) while maintaining that most substantial attitudes (beliefs, standing desires) remain interpretive—preserving a mostly-interpretivist position
promise_reason: Another regress argument against interpretivism; similar to thesis 4 and 8, covering familiar anti-interpretivist ground.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved not because self-interpretation is privileged but because self-ascription itself constitutes a distinctive kind of evidence that other-ascription cannot access—not evidence about a prior state, but evidence that partly brings the state into determinate existence.
sketch: The debate assumes attitudes have determinate content prior to and independent of self-ascription, making self-ascription either observation (undermined by confabulation data) or interpretation (losing authority). But many attitudes—especially higher-order ones like intentions and normative beliefs—are metaphysically indeterminate until articulated. Self-ascription doesn't report or interpret a fully formed state; it crystallizes it. This explains asymmetry without requiring privileged access: when you self-ascribe believing P, you're not merely reporting but also settling what you believe, creating evidence unavailable to third parties. The key premise is that mental states can be metaphysically vague in content until self-interpretation resolves them, similar to how quantum states are indeterminate until measured, but without requiring consciousness to play a constitutive role for all attitudes.
target: The shared assumption across both transparency theorists (Moran) and interpretivists (Carruthers, Gopnik) that attitudes have determinate contents prior to our epistemic access to them
risk: Cannot adequately distinguish between genuine self-knowledge and self-deception or rationalization—if self-ascription constitutes the attitude, how can we be wrong about our own minds in the systematic ways confabulation studies demonstrate?
promise_reason: Self-ascription crystallizing indeterminate states is well-covered territory.

thesis: Holding that self-interpretation and other-interpretation use the same evidence commits you to denying that avowals can be insincere, which interpretivist theorists implicitly reject when they distinguish lying from confabulation.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers and Gopnik claim we know our minds through the same interpretive process we use for others, applied to our own behavior and circumstances. But this entails that avowal ('I believe P') has the same relationship to belief-states as third-person attribution does. When interpreting others, we can recognize insincere reports—they're lying, not merely wrong. But if I have no special access to my beliefs beyond behavioral interpretation, then my saying 'I believe P' is just more behavior to be interpreted. I cannot then coherently distinguish between lying about my belief (which requires knowing what I believe independently of my avowal) and confabulating about it (being wrong). Yet interpretivists clearly maintain this distinction—they treat confabulation as epistemic failure, not deception. This reveals they're implicitly committed to some form of privileged access after all.
target: Strong interpretivism (Carruthers, Gopnik) that denies any epistemic asymmetry between first and third-person attribution
risk: Interpretivists might bite the bullet and reconstruct the lying/confabulation distinction in purely third-personal terms (lying is when behavioral evidence suggests you have second-order knowledge of the first-order state), though this seems to reintroduce the very asymmetry they deny.
promise_reason: The lying/confabulation distinction is interesting but interpretivists have responses available (lying requires meta-interpretive capacity); the internal tension is overstated.

thesis: The asymmetry between self-ascription and other-ascription exists but has the wrong explanation: it derives not from epistemic privilege but from pragmatic immunity—social norms make challenging first-person avowals conversationally costlier than challenging third-person attributions, creating apparent authority that is actually just conventional deference.
sketch: Both sides treat first-person authority as an epistemic phenomenon requiring epistemic explanation (either privileged access or rational agency). But the asymmetry might be purely pragmatic. In normal discourse, contradicting someone's self-ascription ('No, you don't really believe that') carries higher social costs than contradicting other-ascription ('No, she doesn't really believe that'). This isn't because speakers have better evidence about themselves, but because self-ascriptions have a performative element: challenging them questions the speaker's sincerity or rationality, not just accuracy. We treat avowals as authoritative by default because the pragmatic costs of rejection are high, not because they're epistemically secure. The confabulation literature then shows this conventional authority is unjustified—we defer to avowals more than accuracy warrants. The key premise is that conversational norms can create apparent epistemic asymmetries.
target: The shared assumption that first-person authority requires an epistemic explanation rather than a merely pragmatic one
risk: Cannot explain why we ourselves treat our past self-ascriptions as authoritative in private reasoning where social costs are absent, or why there are some contexts (psychotherapy, philosophy) where challenging avowals is conversationally licensed yet the asymmetry persists.
promise_reason: Pragmatic explanations of authority have been explored; while the conversational-cost angle is specific, it doesn't sufficiently explain why these norms exist or why they're so robust.

thesis: The interpretive theorists' own position is unstable: if we really self-attribute through interpretation of behavioral evidence, then the confabulation literature shows we should have no more confidence in our self-attributions than in attributions to others, yet interpretive theorists themselves exhibit first-person authority in their theorizing.
sketch: Carruthers and Gopnik argue we know our minds through interpretation just as we know others' minds, relying on confabulation studies to undermine privileged access. But the key premise is that if this were true, the rational response would be systematic self-doubt — treating one's own self-attributions as no more credible than attributions from observers who have the same behavioral evidence. Yet interpretive theorists don't actually adopt this stance; when they assert 'I believe interpretation explains self-knowledge' they don't qualify it with 'but an observer might be equally warranted in attributing to me the belief that it doesn't.' Their practice reveals a commitment to first-person authority even while their theory denies it. Either they must adopt radical self-doubt (making their own theorizing self-undermining) or admit that interpretation-based self-knowledge has some feature that preserves asymmetry.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's mindreading-based interpretation model
risk: Interpretive theorists might bite the bullet and embrace the self-doubt, or argue that their theory only applies to certain attitudes and not to the theoretical beliefs they express, creating a principled partition.
promise_reason: The performative contradiction charge is familiar from debates about self-refutation; interpretivists can respond that theoretical self-ascription has different standards than ordinary cases.

thesis: The asymmetry between self- and other-attribution survives the interpretive turn because self-interpretation has exclusive access to experienced reasons while other-interpretation must infer them, and attitudes are individuated partly by the reasons that rationalize them from the first-person perspective.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers are committed to the claim that if we know our attitudes through interpretation of evidence, then any asymmetry must derive from different evidence sets available to self vs. other. But they overlook that one crucial type of evidence—experienced reasons (the considerations that feel like reasons to me in deliberation)—is available only first-personally, not through any amount of behavioral observation. Moreover, attitude individuation is partly constituted by rational relations to reasons, not just by functional role. When I interpret my donation as expressing belief that charity X is effective, I'm not just reading off behavior; I'm identifying which reasons I experienced as motivating. Others can hypothesize about my reasons but cannot experience them. This grounds an ineliminable asymmetry: self-attribution individuates attitudes more finely because it has access to experienced rational relations that behavior underdetermines.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's claim that the interpretive model undermines first-person authority by making self- and other-knowledge merely quantitatively different (more evidence vs. less)
risk: The notion of 'experienced reasons' may itself require privileged access to explain, creating circularity; or experienced reasons might be just as subject to confabulation as the attitudes they supposedly individuate
promise_reason: The experienced-reasons asymmetry has been discussed; while the attitude-individuation angle adds something, interpretivists have responses about functional role being sufficient for individuation.

thesis: First-person authority is unstable: it necessarily collapses into either discredited Cartesian infallibility or mere difference in evidence-gathering efficiency, because any middle position requires simultaneously claiming both that self-interpretation is epistemically special and that it can systematically err—a combination that cannot be coherently maintained.
sketch: Moran, Bar-On, and moderate interpretivists all seek a middle ground: rejecting Cartesian infallibility while preserving something distinctively authoritative about self-knowledge. But this position is unstable. If self-knowledge can err (as confabulation shows), then whatever makes it authoritative must be something other than reliability or accuracy. The usual candidates—immediacy, non-inferentiality, special evidence access—all reintroduce the epistemic privilege that interpretivism denies. If instead authority means something non-epistemic (like Moran's deliberative stance), then it's unclear why we should call systematically unreliable self-attributions 'knowledge' at all, or why others should defer to them. The moderate position requires 'authority without reliability,' but authority in any recognizable epistemic sense just is a matter of being reliably right. Any account that grants the empirical findings about confabulation while insisting on preserved authority must either redefine authority into insignificance or smuggle back Cartesian assumptions.
target: The moderate positions of Moran, Bar-On, and anyone trying to preserve first-person authority while accepting interpretivism
risk: May simply be trading on an ambiguity in 'authority' rather than showing genuine instability; the distinction between epistemic and practical/normative authority might be more robust than the argument suggests
promise_reason: The instability argument is forceful but the dilemma is too stark—moderate positions can distinguish types of authority or accept limited, non-Cartesian epistemic privilege.

thesis: Confabulation studies demonstrate not that self-interpretation is pervasive but that first-person authority is question-relative: we have authority about whether we φ but not about why we φ, undermining the assumption that self-knowledge is an all-or-nothing epistemic relation to a mental state.
sketch: Nisbett & Wilson's subjects accurately reported choosing the rightmost stockings but confabulated explanations for why. This pattern recurs: accurate introspective reports of attitudes, poor reports of their etiology. The debate misreads this as showing attitudes themselves are interpretationally accessed. Instead, the data show we have non-interpretive access to THAT we prefer X, intend Y, believe Z (the attitude itself), but must interpret WHY (the attitude's causal history). First-person authority holds for the former, not the latter. The key premise: an attitude is individuated by its content and force (believing-that-P), not by its causal history; confabulation studies probe causal self-knowledge, not attitudinal self-knowledge. Moran is right that we have authority, interpretivists are right that we confabulate—they're just talking past each other about different questions.
target: Both interpretivists who use confabulation data to argue against first-person authority globally, and expressivists who must explain away the confabulation data
risk: The that/why distinction may not be stable—perhaps knowing that I believe P without knowing why commits me to a belief individuation scheme (narrow content?) that's independently problematic, or perhaps some attitudes are constituted by their etiology
promise_reason: The what/why distinction is valuable but arguably already recognized in careful work; presenting it as resolving the debate overstates its novelty and force.

thesis: Accepting first-person authority while embracing interpretive access commits you to an implausible asymmetry: you must hold that self-interpretation is simultaneously more error-prone than other-interpretation (per confabulation studies) yet yields stronger epistemic authority, which is coherent only if authority and reliability come apart more radically than anyone in the debate accepts.
sketch: Interpretivists like Gopnik claim symmetry: we know ourselves like we know others, via interpretation. But they want to preserve some first-person authority. Meanwhile, confabulation studies show we're systematically worse at self-interpretation than the debate assumes (we explain our choices post-hoc, confabulate reasons, etc.). Others observing our behavior plus context often predict our attitudes better than we do. So if self-knowledge is interpretive, and self-interpretation is less reliable than other-interpretation, yet we grant first-person authority, we're committed to authority being independent of reliability. The key premise: no participant in the debate actually accepts this independence—even Bar-On's neo-expressivism grounds authority in a special epistemic access. Interpretivists who want to keep authority must either abandon the interpretive symmetry thesis or embrace that I can have authority about my beliefs despite you knowing them better than I do.
target: Interpretivist positions (Gopnik, Carruthers) that attempt to preserve some form of first-person authority while maintaining the interpretive symmetry thesis
risk: Interpretivists might bite the bullet and accept that first-person authority is merely social/conventional rather than epistemic, or they might argue the confabulation studies show narrow failures that don't generalize to reliability differences overall
promise_reason: The reliability-authority gap is real but the argument that no one accepts this separation is empirically false—some pragmatist positions explicitly embrace it.

thesis: The agentialist view that self-knowledge involves rational settlement rather than discovery collapses into the interpretivist position it opposes, because rational settlement is itself a process of interpreting which commitments best cohere with one's existing attitudes and values—Moran's deliberative transparency is just interpretation with a first-person practical spin.
sketch: Moran argues that answering 'Do I believe P?' by considering whether P (not by introspecting) preserves first-person authority through rational agency: I settle what to believe, not discover what I believe. But this settlement process requires me to survey my existing commitments, values, and evidence to determine whether I should believe P—this IS interpretation, just interpretation aimed at coherence rather than causal explanation. When I deliberate whether P, I'm interpreting which doxastic stance best fits my overall evaluative and cognitive economy. The key premise: any process that takes existing mental states as input and yields a verdict about one's current attitudes via coherence-assessment is interpretive in the relevant sense, even if it's also agentive. The difference between Moran and Carruthers isn't discovery vs. settlement but backward-looking vs. forward-looking interpretation. Agentialism thus doesn't escape the interpretive turn—it just redescribes it in agential vocabulary.
target: Moran's agentialist account and those who treat the deliberative/transparency approach as a genuine alternative to interpretivism
risk: Moran might successfully argue there's a metaphysical difference between constituting one's attitude through deliberation versus discovering a pre-existing attitude through interpretation, even if both involve coherence-reasoning—the direction of fit differs
promise_reason: The claim that agentialism collapses into interpretivism underestimates the difference between forward-looking normative settlement and backward-looking causal interpretation—agentialists have responses.

thesis: First-person authority for beliefs derives not from privileged epistemic access but from the fact that avowing a belief constitutively alters its rational standing in ways that observing it cannot.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be grounded in either superior evidence (perception models) or retained despite equal evidence (expressivist/agentialist models). But this misses how self-ascription itself changes what rational relations the belief has. When I say 'I believe P,' I undertake a rational commitment to P and to defending it that I don't undertake when merely observing behavioral evidence. This commitment-transformation explains why self-ascriptions have distinctive rational force without requiring either privileged access or mysterious expressivist mechanisms. The authority isn't about knowing better—it's about doing something different that generates new rational requirements.
target: The shared assumption between interpretivists and anti-interpretivists that authority must be explained by epistemic superiority or retained despite epistemic parity
risk: May collapse into Moran's agentialism if the rational commitment story just is his deliberative self-knowledge view, or may fail to explain cases where self-ascription seems purely reportive rather than commitment-involving
promise_reason: Avowal altering rational standing is standard expressivist/agentialist territory.

thesis: Interpretivist accounts can explain first-person authority once we recognize that agents have preferential interpretive access to their own standing intentions, which serve as evidence unavailable to external interpreters.
sketch: The interpretive turn assumes all evidence available to self-interpretation is in principle available to others (behavior, context, etc.). But standing intentions—the dispositional states that structure our ongoing projects—are both (a) genuinely attitudinal states requiring interpretation rather than observation, and (b) evidentially available to the agent in a way they aren't to others, because the agent knows what she's trying to do across time in a way that no momentary behavioral slice reveals. These aren't occurrent thoughts (which would return us to inner perception) but standing commitments that the agent interprets her occurrent states against. This preserves the interpretive insight while explaining asymmetry: we interpret ourselves using evidence others lack.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's claim that interpretive evidence is symmetrically available to self and others
risk: Standing intentions might themselves require the very kind of privileged access the view was meant to avoid, or they might turn out to be just as inferable from long-term behavioral patterns observable by others
promise_reason: Standing intentions as special evidence is a familiar move; the claim that they're interpretive yet privileged doesn't clearly escape existing objections to hybrid views.

thesis: First-person authority survives the interpretive turn not because self-interpretation is epistemically privileged, but because the act of self-interpretation itself constitutes a second-order commitment that changes what attitudes the subject has.
sketch: The debate assumes a discovery model: either I discover my attitudes through inner perception or through self-interpretation. But self-interpretation is performative for second-order attitudes. When I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation—if sincere—constitutes a second-order endorsement of P that itself counts as a belief-like state with distinctive rational commitments. The asymmetry between self and other isn't epistemic but constitutive: your interpretation of me can't make me committed to anything, but my interpretation of myself creates new rational obligations. This preserves authority (I determine what I'm committed to defending) while accepting that first-order attitudes may be interpretively accessed. The key premise is that sincere self-ascription is a speech act that creates normative, not just descriptive, facts.
target: Both Carruthers/Gopnik (who treat self-interpretation as purely epistemic) and Moran (who locates authority in transparency to reasons rather than in the self-ascriptive act itself)
risk: This may collapse into a version of Moran's view if the constitutive self-ascription just is deliberative transparency; or it may fail to explain authority about attitudes we disavow upon interpretation
promise_reason: Self-interpretation constituting second-order commitment is familiar ground.

thesis: Confabulation studies show not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically mistake causal-explanatory questions ('Why did I do that?') for constitutive ones ('What attitude did I act from?'), and only the latter questions admit of genuine first-person authority.
sketch: Nisbett and Wilson's studies show people are poor at identifying causal influences on their behavior, but interpretivists wrongly infer that we therefore lack privileged access to our attitudes themselves. The distinction collapses two questions: (1) What is my attitude? versus (2) What caused my attitude or behavior? We have first-person authority only about (1). When subjects confabulate about why they preferred certain stockings, they may still know non-interpretively that they preferred those stockings. The error lies in causal self-explanation, not attitude self-ascription. This explains the data pattern: we err when reconstructing causal histories but can still authoritatively report our current attitudes. The key premise is that attitudes can be introspectively accessible even when their causal genesis is not.
target: Both empirically-minded interpretivists and critics of introspection who treat confabulation studies as undermining all first-person authority
risk: The distinction may be unstable—arguably, knowing 'I believe P' requires some grasp of why I believe it, and the constitutive/causal line blurs in cases like implicit bias where the attitude itself is partly constituted by its causal profile
promise_reason: The constitutive/causal distinction as response to confabulation is already prominent in the literature; this restates rather than advances that move.

thesis: The confabulation literature shows not that we lack introspective access but that we systematically misidentify which mental states are attitudinal (contentful beliefs/desires) versus which are non-attitudinal (trained dispositions, affective colorings), and first-person authority holds only for genuinely attitudinal states.
sketch: Nisbett-Wilson subjects confabulate not about their beliefs but because they mistake trained response dispositions for belief-based actions. When the stockings experiment subject says 'I chose these because of quality,' they're not misreporting a belief but wrongly categorizing a non-doxastic disposition as doxastic. Genuine attitudes are constituted by their role in practical reasoning and linguistic behavior; dispositions shaped by priming or implicit bias lack this rational integration. The key premise is that the attitude/disposition boundary is not given transparently, and interpretive work is needed to classify our own mental states into kinds, but once correctly classified as attitudinal, those states are authoritative because they're partly constituted by rational self-conception.
target: Schwitzgebel's claim that we're unreliable about beliefs generally, and Carruthers' unified interpretive account that treats all self-ascription symmetrically with other-ascription
risk: The attitude/disposition distinction may itself require the kind of privileged access being denied; unclear how we reliably make this classification if we're interpretively fallible
promise_reason: Restricting authority to properly attitudinal states is a standard defensive move; the attitude/disposition boundary claim doesn't add enough novelty.

thesis: The interpretive account collapses into a form of access theory once we recognize that what we have privileged access to is not our attitudes themselves but our interpretive dispositions—the specific patterns of rationalization we're disposed to offer.
sketch: Interpretivists like Carruthers claim we know our minds through interpretation, not access. But interpretation requires stable inputs to interpret—the interpreter needs access to something (behavior, context, rationalization patterns). The key premise: our distinctive first-person perspective comes from immediate, non-interpretive access to which rationalizations we find compelling, which confabulations we're drawn to produce. This is still privileged access, just not to the attitudes themselves. The interpretivist position is unstable because it must either (a) admit we have non-interpretive access to our interpretive tendencies, collapsing back into an access view, or (b) claim interpretation goes 'all the way down,' leading to infinite regress. The asymmetry between self- and other-ascription is explained by direct access to our own interpretive dispositions while only having indirect access to others'.
target: Pure interpretivist accounts like Carruthers and Gopnik that claim to eliminate privileged access entirely
risk: The notion of 'access to interpretive dispositions' might be too thin to ground genuine first-person authority, or might itself require interpretation, blocking the argument
promise_reason: The move to 'access to interpretive dispositions' feels like relabeling rather than resolving the tension between access and interpretation.

thesis: First-person authority for attitudes survives interpretation not because self-knowledge has a special epistemic status, but because self-ascription has a constitutive role that other-ascription lacks: avowing a belief makes it the case that one has committed to it in a way that transforms the epistemic situation itself.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be explained either by special epistemic access or shown to be illusory. But this ignores how speech acts of self-ascription operate. When I say 'I believe that p,' I'm not just reporting a pre-existing state but undertaking a commitment, making myself answerable to p's truth and to coherence requirements in a way that changes what attitudes I can intelligibly be attributed. Other-ascriptions don't have this constitutive dimension—they aim to track what's already there. This explains the asymmetry without requiring special access: I have authority not because I see better, but because my avowals partially constitute the rational position I occupy. The key premise is that attitudes are individuated partly by rational commitments, and self-ascription is the mechanism through which subjects bind themselves to such commitments.
target: The shared assumption between interpretivist and expressivist camps that first-person authority must be explained by the quality of epistemic access (whether privileged or merely different in kind from third-person access)
risk: This may collapse into a form of expressivism that Bar-On already defends, or it may work only for 'transparent' attitudes like belief while failing for desires, intentions, or especially implicit attitudes where avowal seems less constitutive
promise_reason: The constitutive role of avowal is already central to existing literature; this restates rather than advances the position.

thesis: The confabulation literature undermines first-person authority for occurrent conscious states but actually supports it for standing dispositional attitudes, because interpretation operates over different timescales: immediate self-reports are unreliable exactly because they short-circuit the interpretive integration that grounds genuine self-knowledge.
sketch: Current debates treat 'attitudes' monolithically, but Nisbett-Wilson style confabulation studies target immediate reasons for actions and reactions—occurrent, conscious episodes. Standing beliefs and intentions, however, are individuated by patterns over time, and here interpretive methods actually give subjects an advantage: they have access to more data points, experience the phenomenology of deliberation from the inside, and can observe their own patterns of inference in a way that episodic snapshots miss. The interpretive turn threatens first-person authority only if we misconceive attitudes as episodic mental states rather than dispositional patterns. What subjects confabulate about is their occurrent reasoning; what they can know through interpretation is their standing commitments. The key premise is that attitudes are fundamentally dispositional and that interpretive access to one's own pattern-generating mechanisms (even if not introspectively transparent) is richer than external behavioral interpretation allows.
target: Both Carruthers and Schwitzgebel, who use confabulation data to undermine first-person authority generally without distinguishing standing attitudes from occurrent episodes
risk: The distinction may not be sharp enough—standing attitudes arguably just are collections of dispositions to have occurrent states, and if we can't know the latter we can't know the former; also unclear whether subjects really do track their own patterns better than external observers
promise_reason: The occurrent/standing distinction is familiar and the claim that interpretation favors subjects for standing attitudes needs more support.

thesis: First-person authority is preserved not despite interpretation but through it: the interpretive resources available to self-ascription are constitutively richer than those available to other-ascription because only in the self-directed case does the interpretation itself partly constitute what is being interpreted.
sketch: The debate assumes interpretation either preserves authority (somehow) or undermines it. But this presupposes interpretation is a neutral process that either succeeds or fails to track pre-existing facts. Instead, for attitudinal states, self-interpretation is performative in a way other-interpretation cannot be. When I interpret myself as believing P, this very act of endorsement can crystallize an inchoate dispositional state into a determinate belief. The key premise is that many of our attitudes exist in a superposed or indeterminate state until self-ascription forces a collapse. This explains asymmetry without retreating to direct access: I have authority not because I perceive better, but because my interpretation does constitutive work that yours cannot. This draws on but radicalizes Moran's commitment-based view by making the constitution bidirectional and ongoing rather than forward-looking only.
target: The shared assumption of both transparent-access theorists and interpretivists like Carruthers that attitudes are determinate prior to and independent of self-ascription
risk: This might collapse into a form of idealism about attitudes where they have no existence independent of self-interpretation, making systematic self-deception impossible and undermining the empirical findings that motivated the interpretive turn
promise_reason: The performative interpretation idea overlaps substantially with thesis 0 and existing constitutive accounts without clear added value.

thesis: The confabulation literature shows not that we lack first-person authority but that first-person authority operates at the level of rational commitment rather than causal etiology: we have authority about what we're committed to believing, not about why we believe it.
sketch: Nisbett and Wilson show we confabulate about reasons and causes, but this gets wrongly generalized to all self-knowledge. Draw a principled distinction between authority over one's commitments (what I stand for, what I endorse) versus authority over one's causal-explanatory profile (what actually drives my behavior). The Moran-style agentialist is right that I determine what I believe through deliberation about what to believe, but wrong to think this deliberative stance gives me causal-historical knowledge. The interpretivist is right that causal self-knowledge is inferential, but wrong to extend this to normative self-knowledge. The key premise is that 'belief' in the committal sense and 'belief' in the causal-dispositional sense are genuinely distinct kinds, and first-person authority attaches only to the former. This explains why confabulation studies undermine some self-knowledge claims without undermining the asymmetry Bar-On and Moran identify.
target: Both sides treat 'belief' univocally and assume first-person authority must be all-or-nothing across all aspects of our attitudinal states
risk: The distinction might be unstable because commitments that systematically float free from causal dispositions aren't really beliefs at all, just wish-fulfillment, making this a Pyrrhic victory for first-person authority
promise_reason: The commitment/etiology distinction has been made before; this application to confabulation is competent but not novel.

thesis: The interpretive alternative fails because interpretation of others and interpretation of self face opposite directions in evidential time: self-interpretation is necessarily retrospective while other-interpretation can be prospective.
sketch: Carruthers and Gopnik assume self-interpretation and other-interpretation use the same evidence symmetrically. But consider forming an intention right now. When you self-ascribe 'I intend to φ,' you're interpreting evidence that exists only up to this moment, and the intention itself shapes future evidence. When I ascribe an intention to you, I can use evidence from after your self-ascription to test it. This temporal asymmetry means self-interpretation is hostage to future confirmation in a way other-interpretation isn't. The confabulation literature actually supports this: subjects confabulate precisely when asked to explain actions before completing them. This shows self-interpretation can't simply be other-interpretation turned inward, because the evidential base has a fundamentally different temporal structure.
target: Carruthers and Gopnik's symmetry thesis between self and other interpretation
risk: The temporal difference might be merely pragmatic rather than constitutive, or might apply only to forward-looking attitudes like intentions but not beliefs
promise_reason: The temporal-direction claim is confused—other-interpreters also interpret past evidence, and self-interpretation can use prospective evidence; the asymmetry doesn't hold as stated.

thesis: First-person authority depends not on privileged epistemic access but on constitutive authority: self-ascriptions of belief partly constitute what one believes, making them self-fulfilling in a way other-ascriptions cannot be.
sketch: The debate assumes first-person authority must be epistemic authority—better knowledge of pre-existing mental states. But self-ascriptions can have constitutive force: when I sincerely avow 'I believe P,' I thereby commit myself to P in ways that partially determine what I believe, not merely report it. This explains the asymmetry without requiring special access. The key premise: belief is not a purely descriptive psychological state but partly constituted by one's rational commitments and self-conceptions. Other-ascriptions lack this constitutive power because they don't engage the subject's rational agency. This preserves Moran's insight about the deliberative stance while accepting the interpretive turn—we do interpret ourselves, but self-interpretation has world-to-mind direction of fit where other-interpretation has mind-to-world.
target: The shared assumption by both access theorists and interpretivists that first-person authority must be a species of epistemic privilege about antecedently determinate facts
risk: Cannot adequately handle cases of self-deception or unconscious beliefs, where the constitutive story seems to give self-ascriptions too much power to determine reality against recalcitrant evidence
promise_reason: This is essentially a restatement of constitutive authority without adding new elements.
